  • Multi-tenant isolation for fine-tuned adapters and private assets.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Bound concurrency to GPU/API quotas.
  • Batch when throughput matters; stream when UX needs first byte/frame.
  • Prefer latent / distilled models when latency SLOs are tight.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Track cost per successful output (not per request alone).
  • Smaller distilled models for high-QPS paths; premium models for paid tiers.
  • Quotas per user/tenant; alert on burn anomalies.

docs.title: Security & Safety
docs.text:
• Treat prompts and uploaded media as untrusted input.
  • Run content policy checks pre- and post-generation for the modality.
  • Prevent training-data exfiltration and voice/face misuse with policy + detection.
  • Separate credentials for training vs inference.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Alignment Across Modalities is a core topic in Generative AI engineering: understanding how alignment across modalities works, when to use it, and how to ship it safely with measurable quality.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
Teams that skip alignment across modalities ship demos that fail on quality, cost, latency, or safety under real traffic.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Use case How this applies Product feature Ship alignment across modalities as a user-facing capability Internal tool Creative ops, synthetic data, or prototyping Research transfer Port papers into a controlled experiment

docs.title: Core Ideas
docs.text:
1. Define success metrics for alignment across modalities before tuning models.
  2. Prefer the simplest stack that meets the bar (shared or connected encoders + generative heads).
  3. Version data, checkpoints, prompts/conditioning, and safety policy together.
  4. Evaluate offline, then monitor online regressions.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
At a high level, alignment across modalities sits in the GenAI loop: condition → sample → filter → measure.

flowchart TB
  Text --> Fusion
  Image --> Fusion --> Out[Generated modality]

Map each node to an owner in your team (model, platform, product, safety). Ambiguous ownership is how silent regressions ship.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Scenario: You need alignment across modalities in a production feature with a clear success bar.

  1. Write a one-page spec: input modality, output modality, latency SLO, safety policy, and offline metrics.
  2. Pick a baseline model/API and freeze a golden eval set (even 50–200 examples help).
  3. Tune sampling/conditioning only against that set; log seeds and parameters.
  4. Add filters and rate limits before widening traffic.
  5. Canary to 5% users; watch quality + cost + abuse signals; keep one-click rollback.

Example outcome: A baseline that is “good enough” with guardrails beats a flashy model with no eval.

docs.title: Python Examples
docs.text:
def multimodal_generate(inputs: dict, target: str) -> dict:
    return {"inputs": list(inputs), "target": target}

Wire the stub to your real provider (Diffusers, Torch, OpenAI, ElevenLabs, etc.) behind an interface so tests do not hit paid APIs in CI.

docs.title: Training & Data Notes
docs.text:
• Prefer licensed / consented data; document provenance.
  • Deduplicate and filter toxic or low-quality samples before FT.
  • Keep a frozen holdout for regression; never train on the golden set.
  • For personalization (faces, voices, brands), require explicit consent and retention limits.

docs.title: Sampling & Inference
docs.text:
• Expose the knobs users/engineers need (seed, steps, guidance, temperature) with sane defaults.
  • Cap max runtime and max output size at the API edge.
  • Cache stable conditioning embeddings when safe.
  • Deterministic modes (DDIM, temp→0) help debugging; stochastic modes help diversity.

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Version model id + conditioning templates + safety policy as one release bundle.
  • Structured logs: request id, seed, latency, token/step counts, filter decisions (redact raw prompts if needed).
  • Feature flags for model swaps and kill switches for abuse spikes.
  • Multi-tenant isolation for fine-tuned adapters and private assets.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Bound concurrency to GPU/API quotas.
  • Batch when throughput matters; stream when UX needs first byte/frame.
  • Prefer latent / distilled models when latency SLOs are tight.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Track cost per successful output (not per request alone).
  • Smaller distilled models for high-QPS paths; premium models for paid tiers.
  • Quotas per user/tenant; alert on burn anomalies.

docs.title: Security & Safety
docs.text:
• Treat prompts and uploaded media as untrusted input.
  • Run content policy checks pre- and post-generation for the modality.
  • Prevent training-data exfiltration and voice/face misuse with policy + detection.
  • Separate credentials for training vs inference.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Layer Examples Automatic FID/KID, CLIP score, WER, BLEU/BERTScore (task-dependent), toxicity Human Side-by-side preference, rubric scores Online Thumbs, edit distance, redo rate, abuse reports

Ship only if offline floors pass and canary online metrics stay within budget.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Spec the modality and SLO before choosing a paradigm.
  2. Keep golden sets small but sacred.
  3. Change one knob at a time (model or sampler or prompt).
  4. Pair every generator with a filter/reranker when risk is non-trivial.
  5. Document failure modes users will actually see (artifacts, hallucinations, deepfakes).

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Judging quality from three cherry-picked samples.
  • No seed logging — cannot reproduce bugs.
  • Ignoring diversity/coverage until customers complain.
  • Shipping without a safety policy for the modality.
  • Fine-tuning on polluted or non-consented data.

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q: How do you choose between GAN, VAE, and diffusion for images?

A: Default to latent diffusion for quality/controllability; consider GANs/distilled models for hard latency; use VAEs as latent backbones or for representation learning. Decide with latency SLO + FID/human pref + team ops cost.

Q: What do you log for a generative request?

A: Request id, model/adapter versions, conditioning hash, sampler hyperparameters, seed, latency, output size, filter decisions, and cost — with PII redaction.

Q: How do you stop a bad GenAI release?

A: Bundle versioning + canary metrics + automatic rollback on quality/safety/cost thresholds + kill switch for the feature flag.

import torch
from torch.distributions import Normal

def reparameterize(mu: torch.Tensor, logvar: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    std = torch.exp(0.5 * logvar)
    eps = torch.randn_like(std)
    return mu + eps * std

def kl_standard_normal(mu: torch.Tensor, logvar: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    # KL(q(z|x) || N(0,I))
    return -0.5 * torch.sum(1 + logvar - mu.pow(2) - logvar.exp(), dim=-1)

Typical stack: temporal diffusion / DiT + consistency constraints.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Text-to-Video is a core topic in Generative AI engineering: understanding how text-to-video works, when to use it, and how to ship it safely with measurable quality.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
Teams that skip text-to-video ship demos that fail on quality, cost, latency, or safety under real traffic.

Generative systems fail loudly in UX when this topic is underspecified: wrong modality assumptions, uncontrolled sampling, or missing eval gates.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Use case How this applies Product feature Ship text-to-video as a user-facing capability Internal tool Creative ops, synthetic data, or prototyping Research transfer Port papers into a controlled experiment

docs.title: Core Ideas
docs.text:
1. Define success metrics for text-to-video before tuning models.
  2. Prefer the simplest stack that meets the bar (temporal diffusion / DiT + consistency constraints).
  3. Version data, checkpoints, prompts/conditioning, and safety policy together.
  4. Evaluate offline, then monitor online regressions.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
At a high level, text-to-video sits in the GenAI loop: condition → sample → filter → measure.

flowchart LR
  Prompt --> VGen --> Frames --> Encode --> Video

Map each node to an owner in your team (model, platform, product, safety). Ambiguous ownership is how silent regressions ship.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Scenario: You need text-to-video in a production feature with a clear success bar.

  1. Write a one-page spec: input modality, output modality, latency SLO, safety policy, and offline metrics.
  2. Pick a baseline model/API and freeze a golden eval set (even 50–200 examples help).
  3. Tune sampling/conditioning only against that set; log seeds and parameters.
  4. Add filters and rate limits before widening traffic.
  5. Canary to 5% users; watch quality + cost + abuse signals; keep one-click rollback.

Example outcome: A baseline that is “good enough” with guardrails beats a flashy model with no eval.

docs.title: Python Examples
docs.text:
def txt2vid(prompt: str, seconds: float = 4.0, fps: int = 24) -> dict:
    return {"prompt": prompt, "frames": int(seconds * fps), "fps": fps}

Wire the stub to your real provider (Diffusers, Torch, OpenAI, ElevenLabs, etc.) behind an interface so tests do not hit paid APIs in CI.

docs.title: Training & Data Notes
docs.text:
• Prefer licensed / consented data; document provenance.
  • Deduplicate and filter toxic or low-quality samples before FT.
  • Keep a frozen holdout for regression; never train on the golden set.
  • For personalization (faces, voices, brands), require explicit consent and retention limits.

docs.title: Sampling & Inference
docs.text:
• Expose the knobs users/engineers need (seed, steps, guidance, temperature) with sane defaults.
  • Cap max runtime and max output size at the API edge.
  • Cache stable conditioning embeddings when safe.
  • Deterministic modes (DDIM, temp→0) help debugging; stochastic modes help diversity.

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Version model id + conditioning templates + safety policy as one release bundle.
  • Structured logs: request id, seed, latency, token/step counts, filter decisions (redact raw prompts if needed).
  • Feature flags for model swaps and kill switches for abuse spikes.
  • Multi-tenant isolation for fine-tuned adapters and private assets.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Bound concurrency to GPU/API quotas.
  • Batch when throughput matters; stream when UX needs first byte/frame.
  • Prefer latent / distilled models when latency SLOs are tight.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Track cost per successful output (not per request alone).
  • Smaller distilled models for high-QPS paths; premium models for paid tiers.
  • Quotas per user/tenant; alert on burn anomalies.

docs.title: Security & Safety
docs.text:
• Treat prompts and uploaded media as untrusted input.
  • Run content policy checks pre- and post-generation for the modality.
  • Prevent training-data exfiltration and voice/face misuse with policy + detection.
  • Separate credentials for training vs inference.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Layer Examples Automatic FID/KID, CLIP score, WER, BLEU/BERTScore (task-dependent), toxicity Human Side-by-side preference, rubric scores Online Thumbs, edit distance, redo rate, abuse reports

Ship only if offline floors pass and canary online metrics stay within budget.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Spec the modality and SLO before choosing a paradigm.
  2. Keep golden sets small but sacred.
  3. Change one knob at a time (model or sampler or prompt).
  4. Pair every generator with a filter/reranker when risk is non-trivial.
  5. Document failure modes users will actually see (artifacts, hallucinations, deepfakes).

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Judging quality from three cherry-picked samples.
  • No seed logging — cannot reproduce bugs.
  • Ignoring diversity/coverage until customers complain.
  • Shipping without a safety policy for the modality.
  • Fine-tuning on polluted or non-consented data.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the GIL? When does it matter for AI apps?

The Global Interpreter Lock allows one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. It matters for CPU-heavy work (embedding batch on CPU, parsing huge JSON). It does not block I/O-bound LLM API calls — use asyncio for concurrent HTTP. Use multiprocessing or offload to C/Rust for CPU parallelism.

Follow-up: How would you parallelize embedding 1M documents?

Chunk into batches; worker processes or a job queue (Celery/RQ); avoid threading for CPU embed.

Q: async def vs def in FastAPI?

async def routes run on the event loop — good for I/O. CPU work in async routes blocks the loop — use run_in_executor or sync def route with thread pool.

Q: Explain generators. Use case in AI?

yield produces lazy sequences — streaming LLM tokens to client without buffering full response in memory.

docs.title: Trick Questions
docs.text:
Q: Is list.append thread-safe?

CPython's GIL makes single append atomic in practice, but compound read-modify-write is not — use locks or queues for shared state.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Q: Write query — top 3 users by message count last 7 days.

SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS msg_count
FROM messages
WHERE created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days'
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY msg_count DESC
LIMIT 3;

Follow-up: Add rolling 7-day average per user?

Window: AVG(COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY date ROWS 6 PRECEDING)

Q: Why index (tenant_id, created_at) for chat logs?

Queries filter by tenant then time range — composite index supports both.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Exposing raw vendor payloads couples clients to OpenAI (or others). A good chat API models threads, messages, and turns as your resources, with authz and pagination.

flowchart LR
  Client --> Threads[/threads]
  Client --> Messages[/threads/id/messages]
  Client --> Turns[/threads/id/turns]

Prerequisites: Request Lifecycle · APIs

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A chat API is the application-level HTTP contract for conversational LLM features: creating threads, appending user messages, running assistant turns, listing history, and managing metadata — independent of any single model vendor.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Thin vendor wrap Product chat API Clients break on vendor change Stable resources No thread authz model Per-thread ACLs Hard to add tools/UX events First-class turn events

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Endpoint Purpose POST /threads Create conversation POST /threads/{id}/turns User message → assistant reply GET /threads/{id}/messages Paginated history POST /threads/{id}/cancel Abort in-flight turn

docs.title: Resource model
docs.text:
• Thread — container with tenant_id, title, model preferences.
  • Message — role, content parts, tool calls, timestamps.
  • Turn — unit of work producing one assistant message (and tool events).
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant API as Chat API
  participant O as Orchestrator
  C->>API: POST /threads/{id}/turns
  API->>O: run turn
  O-->>API: assistant message
  API-->>C: message resource

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text: Accept Idempotency-Key on turn creation to prevent double sends on mobile retries.

docs.title: Mobile retry
docs.text: Client times out, retries same turn with same idempotency key → server returns original assistant message, does not call the model twice.

docs.title: Shared thread
docs.text: Two users in a workspace; API enforces membership before reads/writes.

docs.title: FastAPI sketch
docs.text:
@app.post("/v1/threads")
async def create_thread(user=Depends(auth)):
    thread = await threads.create(tenant_id=user.tenant_id, user_id=user.id)
    return thread

@app.post("/v1/threads/{thread_id}/turns")
async def create_turn(
    thread_id: str,
    body: TurnCreate,
    request: Request,
    user=Depends(auth),
):
    await threads.assert_member(thread_id, user.id)
    key = request.headers.get("idempotency-key")
    return await chat_service.run_turn(user, thread_id, body.message, idem_key=key)

docs.title: Message DTO
docs.text:
class MessageOut(BaseModel):
    id: str
    role: Literal["user", "assistant", "system", "tool"]
    content: str
    created_at: datetime
    tool_calls: list[dict] | None = None

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Version the API (/v1); changelog for message part types.
  • Cursor pagination for messages, not huge offsets.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Index (thread_id, created_at).
  • Avoid loading full history when only appending.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Return usage on turns for client budgeting UIs.
  • Cap message size in the schema.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Membership checks on every thread route.
  • Strip internal tool credentials from message payloads.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Design resources around UX nouns.
  2. Separate create-message from run-turn if offline drafts exist.
  3. Include request_id in error bodies.
  4. Document streaming as the same turn resource with events.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Returning raw OpenAI response JSON to clients
  • No idempotency on turns
  • Unbounded history GET
  • Forgetting soft-delete / retention policies

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text: Q: Why not expose chat.completions directly to the browser? A: It leaks keys/models, skips your authz and persistence, and couples UX to vendor schemas.

docs.title: Streaming and SSE
docs.text: SSE streaming turns long generations into responsive UX — design event types, heartbeats, and completion semantics carefully.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Streaming reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) perception. Server-Sent Events (SSE) are a practical default for browser chat: one-way server push over HTTP.

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant API as API
  participant P as Provider
  C->>API: POST /turns/stream
  API->>P: stream=true
  loop tokens
    P-->>API: delta
    API-->>C: event: token
  end
  API-->>C: event: done

Prerequisites: Sync, Async, and Streaming · Chat APIs

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Streaming over SSE delivers incremental LLM outputs (and tool/progress events) as text/event-stream frames so clients can render tokens before the full completion exists.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Non-streaming Streaming SSE Blank wait Incremental render Simple retries Need cancel + finalize rules One JSON body Event protocol

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Event Payload token text delta tool_start / tool_end tool name, status error code, message done message_id, usage

docs.title: Framing
docs.text: Each SSE event has optional event: name and data: JSON. Send heartbeats as comments (: ping) every N seconds.

docs.title: Finalization
docs.text: Always persist the final assistant message server-side when the provider finishes, even if the client disconnected mid-way (product choice — document it).

docs.title: Backpressure
docs.text: If the client is slow, decide whether to buffer or cancel the provider stream.

docs.title: Proxy idle timeout
docs.text: Without heartbeats, a 60s thinking gap closes the connection. Fix: : ping every 15s + progress events during tools.

docs.title: Tool call mid-stream
docs.text: Emit tool_start so the UI shows "Searching docs…", then resume token events.

docs.title: FastAPI SSE
docs.text:
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
import json

async def event_gen(messages):
    yield f"event: status\ndata: {json.dumps({'phase': 'generating'})}\n\n"
    async for delta in provider.stream(messages):
        yield f"event: token\ndata: {json.dumps({'text': delta})}\n\n"
    yield f"event: done\ndata: {json.dumps({'ok': True})}\n\n"

@app.post("/v1/threads/{tid}/turns/stream")
async def stream_turn(tid: str, body: TurnCreate):
    return StreamingResponse(event_gen(await build(tid, body)), media_type="text/event-stream")

docs.title: Client fetch reader (browser-oriented sketch)
docs.text:
// EventSource is GET-only; for POST use fetch + ReadableStream parser
const res = await fetch(url, { method: "POST", body, headers });
const reader = res.body.getReader();
// parse SSE chunks...

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Standardize event schema across products.
  • Load-test concurrent streams per instance.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Flush early; avoid buffering entire completion.
  • Keep event payloads small.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Cancel provider on client abort when API supports it.
  • Do not retry a finished stream blindly.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Auth on stream start; do not put tokens in query strings.
  • Apply output filters consistent with policy.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Heartbeats.
  2. Terminal done or error always.
  3. Correlate events with message_id.
  4. Document POST+SSE vs EventSource trade-offs.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• No done event
  • Buffering all tokens then sending one event
  • Forgetting CORS/proxy buffering (X-Accel-Buffering: no)
  • Leaking tool secrets in events

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text: Q: Why not always use WebSockets for chat? A: SSE is enough for server-push tokens, simpler with HTTP infra; use WebSockets when you need rich bidirectional mid-stream control.

docs.title: Tool-Calling UX
docs.text: Tool-calling UX must show what the assistant is doing, ask before side effects, and recover gracefully when tools fail.

docs.text:

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Users distrust invisible tool use. Good UX surfaces status, arguments (when safe), confirmations for mutations, and clear failures — while streaming continues around tools.

flowchart LR
  Intent[Model intends tool] --> UI[Show status]
  UI --> Risk{Side effect?}
  Risk -->|yes| Confirm[User confirm]
  Risk -->|no| Run[Execute]
  Confirm --> Run
  Run --> Result[Show result / error]

Prerequisites: Streaming and SSE · Function Calling

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Tool-calling UX is how the product presents, authorizes, and reports LLM-initiated tool invocations — including progress, confirmation, and error states — not only the final natural-language answer.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Hidden tools Explicit tool UX Surprise side effects Informed consent Opaque latency Progress clarity Silent failures Actionable errors

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Tool type UX pattern Read-only search Inline "Searching…" Create ticket Confirm card Refund / delete Strong confirm + reason Multi-tool agent Step timeline

docs.title: Event protocol
docs.text: Emit tool_start, tool_progress, tool_end / tool_error on the stream. Persist tool messages for transcript fidelity.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
For mutating tools, interrupt the loop: return a pending_approval state to the client; resume on POST .../approvals.

sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant UI as UI
  participant API as API
  participant T as Tool
  API-->>UI: tool_start refund
  UI->>U: Confirm?
  U->>UI: Approve
  UI->>API: approval
  API->>T: execute
  API-->>UI: tool_end

docs.title: Misleading success
docs.text: Tool fails; model apologizes vaguely. Better: UI shows tool error banner; model gets structured error and proposes next step.

docs.title: Parallel tools
docs.text: Show multiple progress rows; do not assume sequential-only UI.

docs.title: Approval gate
docs.text:
MUTATING = {"create_refund", "delete_record"}

async def maybe_execute(tool_name, args, ctx):
    if tool_name in MUTATING and not ctx.approved.get(tool_name):
        return {"status": "pending_approval", "tool": tool_name, "args": redact(args)}
    return await runtime.run(tool_name, args, ctx)

docs.title: SSE tool events
docs.text:
yield f"event: tool_start
data: {json.dumps({'name': name})}

"
result = await runtime.run(name, args)
yield f"event: tool_end
data: {json.dumps({'name': name, 'ok': True})}

"

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Catalog tools with UX metadata (mutating?, confirm_copy).
  • Audit log approvals.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Parallelize read-only tools.
  • Timeouts per tool surfaced to UI.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text: • Failed tools still cost model tokens — surface that in analytics.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Never display secrets in tool args UI.
  • Server-side enforce allowlist regardless of UI.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Classify tools by risk.
  2. Structured errors to the model and the UI.
  3. Keep transcripts faithful (tool messages).
  4. Accessibility: status text, not only spinners.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Auto-running refunds
  • Empty UI during 10s tool calls
  • Showing raw stack traces to users
  • Letting the model invent tool names in the UI

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text: Q: Where should tool confirmation live — UI only or server? A: Server must enforce; UI provides the affordance. Never rely on the client alone.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Users hit Stop. Gateways kill idle connections. Workers exceed budgets. Without coordinated cancellation, you pay for orphaned generations and leave threads half-written.

flowchart TB
  UserStop[User Stop] --> API
  APITimeout[API deadline] --> API
  API --> CancelProvider[Cancel provider stream]
  API --> MarkDB[Mark turn cancelled]

Prerequisites: Streaming and SSE · Retries and Timeouts

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Cancellation aborts in-flight LLM work in response to client or system signals. Timeouts are deadlines at each hop (client, API, tool, provider) that trigger cancellation and typed errors.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Missing cancel Consequence Provider continues Wasted $ No UI stop Frustrated users No deadline Stuck workers

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Layer Mechanism Browser AbortController API request disconnect / cancel endpoint Python asyncio.CancelledError / httpx timeout Provider stream close / cancel API when available

docs.title: Deadline propagation
docs.text: Compute an absolute deadline at ingress; pass remaining budget downstream.

docs.title: Cooperative cancellation
docs.text:
Between tool calls, check a cancel flag / event so agent loops stop promptly.

sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant API as API
  participant P as Provider
  U->>API: abort / cancel
  API->>P: close stream
  API->>API: persist status=cancelled
  API-->>U: cancelled ack

docs.title: Stop button
docs.text: UI aborts fetch; API detects disconnect, closes provider stream, saves partial text optionally as cancelled message.

docs.title: Tool longer than budget
docs.text: Tool timeout fires; orchestrator records tool error and either stops or continues per policy.

docs.title: httpx timeout + cancel
docs.text:
import httpx

timeout = httpx.Timeout(connect=5.0, read=60.0, write=10.0, pool=5.0)

async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=timeout) as client:
    async with client.stream("POST", url, json=payload) as resp:
        async for chunk in resp.aiter_bytes():
            if ctx.cancelled:
                await resp.aclose()
                raise asyncio.CancelledError()
            yield chunk

docs.title: FastAPI disconnect
docs.text:
@app.post("/v1/stream")
async def stream(request: Request):
    async def gen():
        async for tok in provider.stream(...):
            if await request.is_disconnected():
                await provider.abort()
                break
            yield format_sse(tok)
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream")

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Define whether partial tokens are persisted.
  • Metrics: cancel rate, orphaned provider calls.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Check cancel between tools, not only on token boundaries.
  • Bound queue wait separately from run timeout.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Track cancelled-but-billed tokens.
  • Prefer providers with cancel support.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Authorize cancel to thread members only.
  • Cancel tokens should not be guessable IDs alone without auth.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Absolute deadlines at the edge.
  2. Typed timeout errors to clients.
  3. Idempotent cancel endpoints.
  4. Test disconnect paths.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Only client-side timeout with server still running
  • Ignoring CancelledError and continuing tools
  • Infinite client spinner with no server deadline
  • Treating cancel as empty 200 OK without status

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text: Q: How do you implement a Stop button end-to-end? A: Client aborts the stream; API detects disconnect or explicit cancel; cooperative checks stop the orchestrator; provider stream is closed; turn marked cancelled; usage recorded.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Early LLM demos collapse API handlers, prompts, vendor SDKs, and DB writes into one file. That works until you need a second model, a second tenant, or an eval harness.

This lesson expands the reference architecture: edges, services, orchestrators, adapters, stores, and hooks — the skeleton every later section hangs on.

flowchart TB
  Edge[API Edge] --> Svc[Application services]
  Svc --> Orch[Orchestrator]
  Orch --> Provider[Model adapter]
  Orch --> Retriever[Retriever]
  Orch --> ToolRuntime[Tool runtime]
  Svc --> Store[(Threads / users / files)]
  Svc --> Obs[Observability / eval hooks]

Prerequisites: Foundations · Backend Engineering

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An LLM app architecture is a layered design where product APIs and domain services orchestrate prompts, retrieval, and tools through provider adapters, with explicit persistence and observability — treating the model as a dependency, not the application.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Without clear architecture With reference layers Vendor lock-in in handlers Swap adapters behind interfaces Untestable prompt strings Pure prompt builders Hidden state in model memory Explicit thread/job stores Blind production Traces, usage, eval hooks

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Application Architecture focus Chat API Thread store + streaming edge + orchestrator Doc QA Retriever + cite-and-generate path Workflow apps Deterministic DAG + LLM steps at nodes Multi-tenant SaaS Tenant context through every layer

docs.title: Core layers
docs.text:
1. API edge — HTTP/SSE, auth, rate limits, request IDs.
  2. Application services — use-cases (start thread, run turn, create job).
  3. Orchestrator — control flow across model, tools, retrieval.
  4. Provider adapters — normalize OpenAI/Anthropic/local/gateway APIs.
  5. Tool runtime — allowlisted functions with authz and timeouts.
  6. Persistence — threads, messages, files, memories, usage.
  7. Observability — traces, metrics, eval sampling.
flowchart LR
  subgraph Edge
    REST[REST/SSE]
  end
  subgraph Domain
    Svc[Services]
    Orch[Orchestrator]
  end
  subgraph Ports
    LLM[LLMPort]
    Tools[ToolPort]
    Mem[MemoryPort]
  end
  REST --> Svc --> Orch
  Orch --> LLM
  Orch --> Tools
  Orch --> Mem

docs.title: Key principles
docs.text:
1. Provider adapters — Isolate vendor SDKs behind interfaces.
  2. Pure prompt builders — Testable functions, not buried strings.
  3. Explicit state — Do not hide critical state only inside the model.
  4. Policy outside the model — AuthZ, quotas, and invariants in code.

docs.title: Scenario — Adding RAG without rewrite
docs.text: Because retrieval sits behind a port, you add a Retriever implementation and an orchestrator path retrieve → generate without touching the chat HTTP schema.

docs.title: Scenario — Dual-vendor failover
docs.text: LLMPort.complete() tries primary adapter; on ProviderUnavailable, secondary adapter. Services stay unaware of vendors.

docs.title: Scenario — Eval harness
docs.text: The same orchestrator runs offline against golden sets by injecting a fake LLMPort — architecture that cannot be tested offline is unfinished.

docs.title: Port + adapter
docs.text:
from typing import Protocol

class LLMPort(Protocol):
    async def complete(self, messages: list[dict], **kw) -> "Completion": ...

class OpenAIAdapter:
    def __init__(self, client): self.client = client
    async def complete(self, messages, **kw):
        resp = await self.client.chat.completions.create(
            model=kw.get("model", "gpt-4o-mini"),
            messages=messages,
            temperature=kw.get("temperature", 0),
        )
        return Completion(text=resp.choices[0].message.content, usage=resp.usage)

docs.title: Service using orchestrator
docs.text:
class ChatService:
    def __init__(self, orch, threads, usage):
        self.orch, self.threads, self.usage = orch, threads, usage

    async def turn(self, tenant_id: str, thread_id: str, message: str):
        history = await self.threads.load(thread_id)
        result = await self.orch.run_turn(history, message)
        await self.threads.append(thread_id, "user", message)
        await self.threads.append(thread_id, "assistant", result.text)
        await self.usage.record(tenant_id, result.usage)
        return result

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Version your architecture decisions (ADR): streaming protocol, idempotency, tool authz.
  • Keep OpenAPI aligned with service contracts, not with raw provider payloads.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Cache embeddings/retrieval independently from generation.
  • Connection-pool provider HTTP clients per process.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Centralize model selection in config/flags, not scattered string literals.
  • Emit per-tenant usage from one place (the adapter or a decorator).

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Never pass raw provider API keys to the browser.
  • Tool runtime must enforce tenant-scoped credentials.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Draw the diagram before adding an agent framework.
  2. One orchestrator API used by HTTP and workers.
  3. Prefer ports/adapters over framework lock-in.
  4. Put business invariants in code, not only prompts.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• God-object 'agent' with no boundaries
  • Business rules only inside prompts
  • Vendor SDK types leaking into REST schemas
  • No persistence for threads/jobs

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q: What is a provider adapter and why use one? A: A thin interface over vendor SDKs so the app can switch models, add failover, and mock LLM calls in tests without rewriting product code.

Q: Where should prompt templates live? A: In pure, versioned builders/modules — not inline in route handlers — so they can be unit-tested and reviewed like code.

docs.text: Draw hard boundaries between HTTP, domain logic, orchestration, tools, and infra — LLM apps rot when those layers collapse.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Layering is not ceremony. It is how you keep prompt changes from breaking auth, and tool changes from breaking billing.

flowchart TB
  API[API / adapters in] --> Dom[Domain services]
  Dom --> Orch[Orchestration]
  Orch --> Infra[Infra adapters out]
  Dom --> DomRules[Invariants / policies]

Prerequisites: LLM App Architecture

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Layers and boundaries in an LLM app separate delivery (HTTP/SSE), domain (product rules), orchestration (model/tool control flow), and infrastructure (vendors, DB, queues) so each can change with minimal blast radius.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Boundary leak Symptom Provider types in API Clients break on vendor change DB queries in orchestrator Untestable loops AuthZ only in UI Tool exploit via API Prompts in route handlers Impossible review/eval

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Boundary Owns API DTOs, authn wiring, status codes, SSE framing Domain Entitlements, thread rules, billing events Orchestration Step order, retries policy application, tool loop Infra SQL, Redis, OpenAI SDK, S3

docs.title: Dependency rule
docs.text:
Inner layers must not import outer frameworks. Domain should not import FastAPI or OpenAI. Orchestrator depends on ports; infra implements ports.

flowchart TB
  subgraph outward
    FastAPI
    OpenAISDK
    Postgres
  end
  subgraph inward
    Domain
    Orch
  end
  FastAPI --> Domain
  Domain --> Orch
  Orch --> Ports
  OpenAISDK -.->|implements| Ports
  Postgres -.->|implements| Ports

docs.title: What stays out of prompts
docs.text:
• Authorization decisions
  • Numeric billing rules
  • "Must never delete production" invariants

Encode those in domain/policy modules; mention them in prompts only as UX guidance, not as the sole enforcement.

docs.title: Refactor smell — chat.py 2k lines
docs.text: Split into routes/chat.py, services/chat_service.py, orch/turn_orchestrator.py, adapters/openai_llm.py, repos/threads.py.

docs.title: Adding MCP tools
docs.text: Tool runtime is an infra adapter; domain only sees ToolPort.execute(name, args, ctx) with authz already applied.

docs.title: Domain policy vs prompt
docs.text:
def assert_can_call_tool(user: User, tool: str) -> None:
    if tool == "refund_charge" and "finance_admin" not in user.roles:
        raise PermissionError("refund_charge denied")

async def execute_tool(user, tool, args):
    assert_can_call_tool(user, tool)  # code enforcement
    return await tool_runtime.run(tool, args)

docs.title: DTO boundary
docs.text:
class ChatTurnRequest(BaseModel):
    thread_id: str
    message: str = Field(max_length=8_000)

# map to domain command — do not pass Request into orchestrator
@dataclass
class RunTurn:
    tenant_id: str
    thread_id: str
    message: str
    request_id: str

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Enforce boundaries in code review checklists.
  • Archunit-style import linters help in large repos.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text: • Boundaries should not mean unnecessary network hops; prefer in-process ports first.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text: • Keep usage accounting at the adapter boundary so every call is metered once.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text: • AuthZ checks belong in domain/tool runtime, not only in the LLM prompt.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Pass commands/DTOs inward, not framework objects.
  2. One module owns prompt templates.
  3. Orchestrator returns domain results; API maps to HTTP.
  4. Write unit tests for domain without network.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Passing Request into orchestrator
  • Importing OpenAI types in Pydantic response models
  • Trusting the model to refuse unauthorized tools
  • Circular imports across layers

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text: Q: Why not put AuthZ instructions only in the system prompt? A: Models can be manipulated or simply fail; authorization must be enforced in trusted code before side effects.

docs.title: Provider Adapters and Gateways
docs.text: Wrap vendors in adapters — and optionally an LLM gateway — so routing, retries, and policy stay under your control.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Raw SDK calls in business logic create lock-in and inconsistent retries. Adapters normalize interfaces; gateways centralize cross-cutting concerns for many services.

flowchart LR
  App[LLM App] --> Adapter[Provider adapter]
  Adapter --> GW[Optional gateway]
  GW --> OAI[OpenAI]
  GW --> Ant[Anthropic]
  GW --> Loc[Local/vLLM]

Prerequisites: Layers and Boundaries

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A provider adapter translates your app's LLMPort into a vendor SDK. An LLM gateway is a shared proxy that adds routing, auth, rate limits, caching, and observability across many callers.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Concern Adapter Gateway Per-app interface Yes Optional Org-wide rate limits Hard Natural fit Central guardrails Possible Strong fit Local unit tests Mock adapter Harder

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Pattern When In-process adapter only Single service, simple fleet Adapter + gateway Many services, shared keys, org policy Gateway-only (HTTP) Polyglot clients; still keep a thin client adapter

docs.title: Adapter responsibilities
docs.text:
• Map messages/tools to vendor schema
  • Normalize usage and finish reasons
  • Apply timeouts and error taxonomy (RateLimited, Unavailable, InvalidRequest)
  • Redact secrets before logging

docs.title: Gateway responsibilities
docs.text:
• API key custody and per-tenant virtual keys
  • Model routing / aliases (chat-strong → concrete model)
  • Cache for identical deterministic requests
  • Global concurrency caps
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as Service
  participant A as Adapter
  participant G as Gateway
  participant V as Vendor
  S->>A: complete(messages, model_alias)
  A->>G: POST /v1/chat/completions
  G->>V: routed call
  V-->>G: response
  G-->>A: normalized JSON
  A-->>S: Completion

docs.title: Alias routing
docs.text: Product asks for model="support-draft". Gateway maps alias → gpt-4o-mini in staging and a larger model in prod via config — no app redeploy for model bumps when alias is stable.

docs.title: Outage failover
docs.text: Primary 503 → gateway retries secondary provider with translated messages (within capability limits).

docs.title: Error taxonomy
docs.text:
class LLMError(Exception): ...
class RateLimited(LLMError): ...
class ProviderUnavailable(LLMError): ...
class InvalidRequest(LLMError): ...

def map_openai_error(exc: Exception) -> LLMError:
    status = getattr(exc, "status_code", None)
    if status == 429:
        return RateLimited(str(exc))
    if status in (500, 502, 503):
        return ProviderUnavailable(str(exc))
    return InvalidRequest(str(exc))

docs.title: Thin HTTP gateway client
docs.text:
import httpx

class GatewayLLM:
    def __init__(self, base_url: str, api_key: str):
        self.client = httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=base_url, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}, timeout=60)

    async def complete(self, messages, model="chat-strong"):
        r = await self.client.post("/v1/chat/completions", json={"model": model, "messages": messages})
        r.raise_for_status()
        data = r.json()
        return data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Own an error taxonomy shared by reliability policies.
  • Version gateway APIs; treat aliases as contracts.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Enable HTTP/2 to providers where available.
  • Connection pooling at adapter/gateway.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Cache only when temperature=0 and inputs identical.
  • Tag spend by alias + tenant at the gateway.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Prefer gateway-held keys over distributing vendor keys to every microservice.
  • Audit model access by tenant.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Normalize finish reasons and tool call shapes.
  2. Keep streaming and non-streaming parity in the adapter.
  3. Contract-test adapters against recorded fixtures.
  4. Document capability gaps across vendors.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Catching all exceptions and retrying invalid requests
  • Logging full prompts at the gateway without redaction
  • Hardcoding model IDs in 20 services
  • Assuming all vendors support the same tool schema

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text: Q: Adapter vs gateway — do you need both? A: Adapters are almost always worth it for testability. Gateways pay off at org scale for key management, routing, and centralized policy.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SaaS LLM products share compute but must never share customer context by accident. Tenancy touches every layer: auth, retrieval filters, tool credentials, rate limits, and billing.

flowchart TB
  Req[Request] --> T[Resolve tenant]
  T --> Q[Quota / plan]
  Q --> Ctx[Tenant config + flags]
  Ctx --> Orch[Orchestrate with tenant scope]
  Orch --> Data[(Tenant-scoped data)]

Prerequisites: LLM App Architecture

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A multi-tenant LLM app serves many customers from one deployment while enforcing tenant isolation for data, configuration, secrets, usage quotas, and observability.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Risk Example Data leak RAG without tenant_id filter Noisy neighbor One tenant exhausts RPM Config bleed Tenant A sees Tenant B prompt experiment Key confusion Shared tool OAuth token across tenants

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Tenancy model Notes Pool (shared DB, row filters) Common SaaS; strict query discipline Silo (per-tenant DB/schema) Higher isolation, more ops Hybrid Sensitive data siloed; chat meta pooled

docs.title: Tenant context object
docs.text:
Carry tenant_id (and optional workspace_id) explicitly through services — do not rely on ambient globals without care.

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant API as API
  participant RAG as Retriever
  participant DB as Vector DB
  C->>API: Bearer token
  API->>API: tenant_id from auth
  API->>RAG: query + tenant_id
  RAG->>DB: search WHERE tenant_id=...
  DB-->>RAG: hits

docs.title: Quotas
docs.text: Enforce RPM, TPM, daily $, and max context size per plan before calling providers.

docs.title: Vector leak regression
docs.text: Engineer adds a debug "search all" path without tenant filter. Mitigation: integration test that inserts two tenants' docs and asserts zero cross hits; code review checklist item.

docs.title: Custom model per enterprise
docs.text: Tenant config selects model_alias and optional BYOK via gateway virtual keys.

docs.title: Tenant-scoped retrieval
docs.text:
async def retrieve(tenant_id: str, query: str, k: int = 5):
    assert tenant_id, "tenant_id required"
    return await vector_db.search(
        collection="docs",
        query=query,
        filters={"tenant_id": tenant_id},
        k=k,
    )

docs.title: Quota check
docs.text:
async def check_quota(tenant_id: str, est_tokens: int) -> None:
    plan = await plans.get(tenant_id)
    used = await usage.tpm(tenant_id)
    if used + est_tokens > plan.tpm_limit:
        raise HTTPException(429, "token quota exceeded")

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Make tenant_id required in repository method signatures.
  • Separate billing accounts from auth tenants carefully (resellers).

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Per-tenant concurrency limits protect shared worker pools.
  • Cache tenant config with short TTL.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Attribute every provider call to tenant + feature flag.
  • Soft and hard limits; notify before hard cutoffs.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Test isolation continuously.
  • Redact tenant data in shared logs; partition traces by tenant attribute.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Thread tenant context via typed TenantContext.
  2. Default-deny on data access.
  3. Per-tenant encryption keys when contracts require.
  4. Load-test noisy-neighbor scenarios.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Global vector search without filters
  • Shared tool credentials across tenants
  • Logging prompts from all tenants to one unscoped bucket
  • Quotas only on the edge, not on workers

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text: Q: How do you prevent cross-tenant RAG leakage? A: Mandatory tenant filters at the retrieval API, defense-in-depth in the vector index metadata, and automated tests that fail the build if cross-tenant hits appear.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Teams often say "we're building an agent" when they mean "we call GPT from a form." That ambiguity drives overbuilt orchestration, fuzzy SLAs, and UI that cannot explain what the system is doing.

This lesson draws hard boundaries between three common shapes so you can pick architecture, UX, and evaluation criteria deliberately.

flowchart LR
  Job[User job] --> Shape{Product shape?}
  Shape -->|Structured task| App[App]
  Shape -->|Conversation| Chat[Chat]
  Shape -->|Multi-step + tools| Agent[Agent]

Prerequisites: Prompt Engineering · Large Language Models

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An LLM product shape is the interaction and control model of your system: a focused app (one job, structured I/O), a chat product (threaded conversation), or an agent (plan + tools + loops with budgets).

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Stakeholder Care-about Product Clear UX promises ("answer in one shot" vs "I'll take a few steps") Engineering Latency budgets, state model, tool authz Ops / SRE Failure modes and cost envelopes Legal / Safety Autonomy boundaries and human-in-the-loop

Wrong shape → wrong reliability story. Agents need step budgets and tool allowlists; chat needs thread persistence and streaming; apps need schemas and idempotent APIs.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Shape Best for Avoid when App Classification, extraction, rewrite, summarization APIs User must negotiate intent over many turns Chat Support, tutoring, copilots with memory of the thread Task is a single form submit with a schema Agent Research, ops assistants, multi-tool workflows A RAG chain or deterministic pipeline would suffice

docs.title: App (single-purpose LLM feature)
docs.text:
An app exposes a contract: typed input → typed (or validated) output. The model is a step inside a service method. State lives in your DB; conversation history is optional or absent.

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant API as App API
  participant O as Orchestrator
  participant M as Model
  C->>API: POST /summarize {doc_id}
  API->>O: build prompt + constraints
  O->>M: completion
  M-->>O: text
  O-->>API: validated summary
  API-->>C: 200 JSON

docs.title: Chat (threaded conversation)
docs.text: A chat product persists messages in a thread, streams tokens, and may call tools — but the primary loop is user turn → assistant turn. Autonomy is bounded by the turn.

docs.title: Agent (goal + tools + control loop)
docs.text: An agent repeatedly plans, calls tools, and observes until a stop condition: goal met, budget exhausted, or human approval required. The UI must surface steps, not only final text.

docs.title: Decision heuristic
docs.text:
1. Can a schema + one model call (or retrieve-then-generate) solve it? → App
  2. Does quality depend on multi-turn clarification or memory of prior turns? → Chat
  3. Do you need open-ended tool use across unknown step counts? → Agent (with hard budgets)

docs.title: Scenario A — Invoice field extraction
docs.text: Finance uploads PDFs and needs {vendor, amount, due_date}. This is an app: structured output, idempotent job IDs, no chat UI.

docs.title: Scenario B — IT helpdesk bot
docs.text: Employees describe issues in natural language; the bot asks clarifying questions and links runbooks. This is chat with optional tool calls (ticket create). Not a free-roaming agent.

docs.title: Scenario C — Cloud cost investigator
docs.text: "Find why spend spiked last week" requires metrics APIs, SQL, and iterative hypotheses. This is an agent with allowlisted tools, max 12 steps, and a human confirm before applying changes.

docs.title: 1. App-style structured call
docs.text:
from openai import OpenAI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

client = OpenAI()

class InvoiceFields(BaseModel):
    vendor: str
    amount: float = Field(ge=0)
    due_date: str  # ISO date

def extract_invoice(text: str) -> InvoiceFields:
    resp = client.beta.chat.completions.parse(
        model="gpt-4o-mini",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "Extract invoice fields. No commentary."},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
        response_format=InvoiceFields,
    )
    return resp.choices[0].message.parsed

docs.title: 2. Chat turn with thread persistence
docs.text:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class ChatTurn(BaseModel):
    thread_id: str
    message: str

@app.post("/v1/chat/turns")
async def chat_turn(body: ChatTurn):
    history = await load_messages(body.thread_id)
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": body.message})
    assistant = await run_chat_completion(history)
    await save_message(body.thread_id, "assistant", assistant)
    return {"thread_id": body.thread_id, "reply": assistant}

docs.title: 3. Agent budget guard
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class AgentBudget:
    max_steps: int = 8
    max_tool_calls: int = 20
    max_tokens: int = 50_000

def should_stop(state: dict, budget: AgentBudget) -> str | None:
    if state["steps"] >= budget.max_steps:
        return "max_steps"
    if state["tool_calls"] >= budget.max_tool_calls:
        return "max_tool_calls"
    if state["tokens"] >= budget.max_tokens:
        return "max_tokens"
    if state.get("done"):
        return "goal_met"
    return None

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Document the shape in the PRD and OpenAPI description.
  • Measure different SLOs: apps (p95 latency), chat (TTFT + full reply), agents (steps to success, tool error rate).

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Apps: optimize prompt size and caching; avoid agent loops.
  • Chat: stream early; truncate history with summarization policies.
  • Agents: parallelize independent tool calls; cache retrieval.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Agents multiply cost by step count — set hard caps and cheaper models for routing.
  • Chat history grows tokens linearly — compress or window.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Apps: validate outputs; treat model text as untrusted.
  • Chat: prompt-injection via user or pasted content.
  • Agents: tool allowlists, least privilege, human approval for side effects.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Name the shape in code (InvoiceExtractionApp, SupportChat, CostAgent).
  2. Prefer apps and chat before agents.
  3. Expose progress for agents; typing indicators for chat; job status for apps.
  4. Evaluate with shape-appropriate datasets.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Calling everything an "agent"
  • Shipping agent UX for a one-shot extraction API
  • No stop conditions on tool loops
  • Hiding tool failures from the user

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Q: How do you decide between a chatbot and an agent? A: If the user drives turn-by-turn conversation and tools are occasional, use chat. If the system must autonomously chain tools toward a goal under budgets, use an agent. Start with the simpler shape.

Q: What breaks if you agentize a classification problem? A: Extra latency, non-determinism, higher cost, and harder evaluation — with no accuracy gain over a structured single call.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Production incidents rarely sit "inside the model." They sit in lifecycle gaps: missing idempotency keys, prompts built after auth checks fail open, streams that never cancel upstream, or traces without correlation IDs.

This lesson maps a reference lifecycle you can implement in FastAPI (or any backend) and adapt for sync, async, and streaming modes.

flowchart TB
  A[Ingress] --> B[AuthN/AuthZ]
  B --> C[Validate + quotas]
  C --> D[Load state / retrieve]
  D --> E[Orchestrate]
  E --> F[Model / tools]
  F --> G[Validate output]
  G --> H[Persist + respond]
  H --> I[Telemetry]

Prerequisites: App vs Chat vs Agent

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The LLM request lifecycle is the ordered set of stages from client ingress to final response (or job completion): authenticate, authorize, validate, assemble context, call models/tools, stream or persist results, and emit telemetry.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Stage skipped Typical failure AuthZ on tools Cross-tenant data leak Input validation Prompt blowups / injection Output validation Broken clients / XSS in UI Cancellation Orphaned provider spend Telemetry Blind debugging

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Mode Lifecycle variant Sync HTTP Single request/response; full completion before 200 Streaming SSE Headers early; tokens as events; final done event Async job 202 + job_id; worker runs lifecycle; client polls/webhooks

docs.title: Reference stages
docs.text:
1. Ingress — TLS terminate, request ID, rate-limit key.
  2. AuthN / AuthZ — user/tenant identity; permission for model feature and tools.
  3. Contract validation — schema, size limits, content policy pre-checks.
  4. Quota / budget — tokens, $ cap, concurrency slots.
  5. State load — thread messages, memories, feature flags.
  6. Context assembly — prompts, RAG, tool schemas (pure functions where possible).
  7. Execution — model calls, tool calls, retries within policy.
  8. Output gate — schema validate, safety filters, PII redaction for logs.
  9. Persistence — messages, usage rows, audit events.
  10. Egress — JSON, SSE, or job status; always attach request_id.
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant E as Edge API
  participant O as Orchestrator
  participant P as Provider
  participant DB as Store
  C->>E: POST /v1/chat (Idempotency-Key)
  E->>E: auth + validate
  E->>DB: load thread
  E->>O: run(turn)
  O->>P: chat.completions
  P-->>O: tokens / tool_calls
  O->>DB: save messages + usage
  O-->>E: result
  E-->>C: response + request_id

Propagate request_id / trace_id to provider metadata, logs, and client headers.

docs.title: Happy path chat turn
docs.text: User sends a message → auth OK → history loaded → model streams → assistant message saved → usage billed to tenant.

docs.title: Partial failure mid-tool
docs.text: Model requests create_ticket → tool succeeds → second tool times out → record partial side effects and return a recoverable error with request_id.

docs.title: Client disconnect
docs.text: Browser closes SSE → API cancels provider stream and marks the turn cancelled.

docs.title: FastAPI request ID middleware
docs.text:
import uuid
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware

app = FastAPI()

class RequestIdMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next):
        rid = request.headers.get("x-request-id", str(uuid.uuid4()))
        request.state.request_id = rid
        response = await call_next(request)
        response.headers["x-request-id"] = rid
        return response

app.add_middleware(RequestIdMiddleware)

docs.title: Orchestrated turn
docs.text:
async def handle_chat_turn(ctx, turn):
    await authorize(ctx, action="chat.write", thread_id=turn.thread_id)
    await check_quota(ctx.tenant_id, estimated_tokens=2_000)
    history = await threads.load(turn.thread_id, limit=40)
    prompt = build_messages(system=flags.system_prompt, history=history, user=turn.message)
    completion = await llm.chat(prompt, model=flags.model, timeout_s=60)
    await threads.append(turn.thread_id, role="user", content=turn.message)
    await threads.append(turn.thread_id, role="assistant", content=completion.text)
    await usage.record(ctx.tenant_id, completion.usage, request_id=ctx.request_id)
    return {"text": completion.text, "request_id": ctx.request_id}

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Make stages explicit in code so new engineers see the contract.
  • Separate mutating stages (tools, DB writes) from pure stages (prompt build).

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Parallelize independent loads (flags + history + entitlements).
  • Avoid serial chatty DB access in the hot path.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Estimate tokens before calling the model; reject oversized contexts early.
  • Record usage even on failures after provider charge.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• AuthZ before retrieval of tenant documents.
  • Never log raw prompts containing secrets; redact.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. One request_id end-to-end.
  2. Timeouts at every I/O boundary.
  3. Document persistence ordering for user/assistant messages.
  4. Treat provider responses as untrusted input to validators.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Calling the model before authz
  • No cancellation on client disconnect
  • Usage not recorded on streaming abort
  • Mixing job lifecycle with HTTP request scope carelessly

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text: Q: What belongs in middleware vs orchestrator? A: Middleware: request IDs, auth parsing, coarse rate limits. Orchestrator: prompt assembly, tool loops, domain rules, persistence of conversation state.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
LLM calls are slow and bursty compared to typical microservice RPCs. Choosing the wrong execution mode causes gateway timeouts, poor UX, or duplicated work.

flowchart TB
  Need[Latency / UX need] --> M{Mode}
  M -->|under ~15s, small payload| Sync[Sync HTTP]
  M -->|long jobs, batch, tools| Async[Async job]
  M -->|chat UX, TTFT matters| Stream[Streaming SSE/WebSocket]

Prerequisites: Request Lifecycle

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An execution mode is how the client waits for LLM work: sync (block until done), async job (enqueue and poll/webhook), or streaming (incremental tokens/events over a long-lived connection).

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Mode Strength Weakness Sync Simple clients, easy retries Proxy timeouts; poor for long tools Async job Survives disconnects; scalable workers More moving parts; eventual consistency Streaming Fast perceived latency Harder cancel/retry; partial failures

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Product Recommended mode Form "rewrite this paragraph" Sync or short stream Chat assistant Streaming SSE "Analyze 200 PDFs" Async job + progress Agent with long tool chains Async job or stream-of-events

docs.title: Sync
docs.text: Client waits; server holds the connection until completion. Keep total time under your edge timeout (often 60s).

docs.title: Async jobs
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant API as API
  participant Q as Queue
  participant W as Worker
  C->>API: POST /jobs
  API->>Q: enqueue
  API-->>C: 202 job_id
  W->>Q: dequeue
  W->>W: run lifecycle
  C->>API: GET /jobs/id
  API-->>C: status + result

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text: Send early bytes (TTFT). Prefer SSE for browser-friendly chat; WebSockets when you need bidirectional cancel/control.

docs.title: Hybrid
docs.text: Stream tokens for language; for long tools, emit progress events, then resume tokens.

docs.title: Gateway timeout
docs.text: A sync agent call runs 90s behind a 60s load balancer → client 502 while the worker still burns tokens. Fix: async job or stream with heartbeats.

docs.title: Mobile flaky network
docs.text: Streaming chat drops mid-reply. Design resume with message_id + last event sequence, or finalize on server and let client refetch.

docs.title: Sync endpoint
docs.text:
@app.post("/v1/rewrite")
async def rewrite(body: RewriteRequest):
    text = await llm.complete(prompt_for(body), timeout_s=30)
    return {"text": text}

docs.title: Async job enqueue
docs.text:
@app.post("/v1/jobs/analyze", status_code=202)
async def analyze(body: AnalyzeRequest, background: BackgroundTasks):
    job_id = new_id()
    await jobs.create(job_id, status="queued")
    background.add_task(run_analyze_job, job_id, body)
    return {"job_id": job_id, "status": "queued"}

docs.title: Streaming tokens
docs.text:
async def stream_tokens(messages: list[dict]):
    stream = await client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=messages, stream=True,
    )
    async for event in stream:
        delta = event.choices[0].delta.content or ""
        if delta:
            yield delta

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Document max duration per mode in the API contract.
  • Heartbeat SSE comments (: ping) to keep intermediaries from closing idle streams.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Streaming improves perceived latency more than total time.
  • Autoscaling async workers on queue depth.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Disconnects mid-stream may still incur provider cost — cancel aggressively.
  • Async retries need idempotency to avoid double spend.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Job status endpoints must be tenant-scoped.
  • Decide buffer-then-filter vs stream-then-risk for safety policies.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Default chat to streaming; batch to async jobs.
  2. Timeouts in clients and servers.
  3. Progress events for multi-step work.
  4. Immutable job results once terminal.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Sync endpoints for multi-minute agents
  • No heartbeat on SSE
  • Retrying non-idempotent sync calls blindly
  • Assuming WebSocket is required for chat

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text: Q: When is SSE preferable to WebSockets for LLM chat? A: When the server primarily pushes tokens and the client rarely sends mid-stream control; SSE is simpler through HTTP proxies and browsers.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Orchestration is the control flow around model calls. Over-orchestrating creates latency and failure surfaces; under-orchestrating pushes too much onto one fragile prompt.

flowchart TB
  Req[Request] --> R{Router}
  R --> Simple[Single LLM call]
  R --> Rag[Retrieve then generate]
  R --> Agent[Tool loop]
  R --> Flow[Deterministic workflow]

Prerequisites: LLM App Architecture · App vs Chat vs Agent

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Orchestration is the control flow around model calls. Patterns include: single-call, chain, router, tool-calling loop, DAG workflow, and human-in-the-loop. Pick the simplest pattern that meets reliability needs.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Pattern mismatch Result Agent for FAQ Slow, flaky, expensive Single call for multi-system ops Hallucinated side effects Unbounded tool loop Runaway cost

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Application Pattern FAQ bot Router + RAG Ops assistant Tool loop with allowlists ETL + summary DAG workflow Form extraction Single-call structured output

docs.title: Pattern catalog
docs.text: Pattern Control Typical stop Single-call One completion Response returned Chain / pipeline Fixed stages Last stage Router Classify then branch Branch completes Tool loop Model selects tools Budget / final answer Graph / DAG Explicit edges Terminal node HITL Pause for human Approval / reject

docs.title: Key principles
docs.text:
1. Simplest winning pattern — Prefer RAG/chain before agents.
  2. Determinism where required — Use code for invariants; LLMs for language.
  3. Timeouts & budgets — Cap steps, tokens, and tool calls.
flowchart LR
  P1[Single] --> P2[Chain]
  P2 --> P3[Router]
  P3 --> P4[Tool loop]
  P4 --> P5[Graph]

docs.title: FAQ that became an agent
docs.text: Team wrapped docs QA in an agent framework. Latency 8s → 25s with no quality gain. Fix: retrieve-then-generate chain + intent router for "talk to human".

docs.title: Ops assistant
docs.text: Allowlist get_logs, restart_service (with approval), max 10 steps — tool loop is justified.

docs.title: Pattern selector
docs.text:
from enum import Enum

class Pattern(str, Enum):
    SINGLE = "single"
    RAG = "rag"
    TOOL_LOOP = "tool_loop"

async def handle(intent: str, payload):
    pattern = await route_intent(intent)
    if pattern == Pattern.SINGLE:
        return await single_call(payload)
    if pattern == Pattern.RAG:
        docs = await retrieve(payload.query)
        return await generate(payload.query, docs)
    return await tool_loop(payload, budget=AgentBudget())

docs.title: Budgeted tool loop sketch
docs.text:
async def tool_loop(payload, budget: AgentBudget):
    messages = build_initial(payload)
    state = {"steps": 0, "tool_calls": 0, "tokens": 0}
    while True:
        reason = should_stop(state, budget)
        if reason:
            return finalize(messages, reason)
        resp = await llm.chat(messages, tools=TOOLS)
        state["steps"] += 1
        if resp.tool_calls:
            for tc in resp.tool_calls:
                state["tool_calls"] += 1
                result = await run_tool(tc)
                messages.append(tool_message(tc, result))
        else:
            return resp.text

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Log which pattern ran per request for debugging.
  • Feature-flag pattern upgrades (chain → agent) carefully.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Parallelize independent retrieval/tools.
  • Short-circuit routers with rules before LLM classifiers when possible.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Measure average steps/tokens per pattern.
  • Use small models for routing.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Allowlists for tools; never 'run arbitrary code' without sandbox.
  • HITL for irreversible actions.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Start single-call; add structure only when eval fails.
  2. Encode budgets in config.
  3. Prefer deterministic graphs for compliance workflows.
  4. Separate routing accuracy metrics from answer quality.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Agentizing a pure retrieval problem
  • Unbounded tool loops without budgets
  • Silent pattern switches in production
  • Mixing HITL and fully automatic paths without UX cues

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text: Q: When do you choose a tool loop over a fixed chain? A: When the set or order of tools cannot be known ahead of time and you can enforce budgets and allowlists. If the steps are fixed, a chain/DAG is simpler and more reliable.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A chain is a linear sequence of stages (retrieve → draft → critique → format). A pipeline emphasizes batch/stream processing with the same idea: explicit stages, typed intermediates, and isolated failures.

flowchart LR
  In[Input] --> S1[Stage 1]
  S1 --> S2[Stage 2]
  S2 --> S3[Stage 3]
  S3 --> Out[Output]

Prerequisites: Orchestration Patterns

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A chain/pipeline is an orchestration style where stages run in a predetermined order, each consuming a validated intermediate artifact from the previous stage.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Benefit Detail Debuggability Fail at stage N with artifact N-1 Eval Score stages independently Caching Reuse retrieval across generations Compliance Prove which steps ran

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Pipeline Stages RAG answer Retrieve → rerank → generate → cite check Content Outline → draft → style → safety Support Classify → retrieve macros → draft reply

docs.title: Stage contract
docs.text:
Each stage declares input/output schemas (Pydantic). The chain runner validates between stages.

flowchart TB
  A[Retrieve Docs] -->|DocsBundle| B[Generate Answer]
  B -->|Draft| C[Validate Citations]
  C -->|Final| D[Return]

docs.title: Fan-out / fan-in
docs.text: Map-reduce summarization: split docs → summarize parts in parallel → reduce summary.

docs.title: Citation checker stage
docs.text: Generation claims doc IDs; validator stage ensures every citation exists in DocsBundle or strips/flags it.

docs.title: Partial reuse
docs.text: User regenerates answer with new tone: reuse cached retrieve/rerank stages; only re-run generate.

docs.title: Simple chain runner
docs.text:
from typing import Callable, Any

async def run_chain(stages: list[Callable], data: Any):
    for stage in stages:
        data = await stage(data)
        # optional: schema validate here
    return data

async def retrieve(ctx): ...
async def generate(ctx): ...
async def cite_check(ctx): ...

result = await run_chain([retrieve, generate, cite_check], ctx)

docs.title: Parallel map stage
docs.text:
import asyncio

async def map_summarize(chunks: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    return await asyncio.gather(*[summarize_one(c) for c in chunks])

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Persist stage artifacts for audit when required.
  • Idempotent stages help retries.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Parallelize independent stages only.
  • Bound concurrency for map stages.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Cache expensive early stages.
  • Use smaller models for outline/classify stages.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Validate untrusted stage outputs before tools.
  • Do not pass raw user PII to every stage if unnecessary.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Name stages and emit spans per stage.
  2. Keep stages under ~1 responsibility.
  3. Prefer code branching over another LLM when rules are crisp.
  4. Golden-test each stage.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Giant mega-prompt instead of stages when eval demands modularity
  • No schema between stages
  • Hidden shared mutable state
  • Unbounded fan-out

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text: Q: Chain vs agent? A: Chains fix control flow in code; agents let the model choose next actions. Use chains when the path is known.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Not every message should hit your strongest model or heaviest workflow. Routers classify intent, risk, or language and dispatch accordingly.

flowchart TB
  U[User message] --> R{Router}
  R -->|billing| B[Billing flow]
  R -->|tech| T[RAG tech docs]
  R -->|abuse| S[Safety path]
  R -->|unknown| F[Fallback clarifier]

Prerequisites: Orchestration Patterns

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A router selects a downstream path (prompt, model, tools, or workflow) based on rules and/or a classifier (often an LLM or smaller model) applied to the request.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Without routing With routing One mega-prompt Specialized prompts Always large model Cheap model for easy intents No safety lane Dedicated abuse handling

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: Signal Route by Intent billing / tech / chitchat Risk high → stronger model + HITL Language locale-specific prompts Tenant plan feature entitlement

docs.title: Layered routing
docs.text:
1. Hard rules — regex, entitlements, maintenance mode.
  2. Lightweight classifier — embeddings/small model.
  3. LLM classifier — structured label + confidence.
  4. Fallback — clarify or general assistant.
flowchart LR
  Rules --> Emb[Embedding classifier]
  Emb --> LLM[LLM classifier]
  LLM --> Dispatch

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text: If confidence < threshold, do not silently guess — ask a clarifying question or use the safe default path.

docs.title: Cost saver
docs.text: 80% of traffic is FAQ → small model RAG. Escalations → large model. Router accuracy becomes a cost KPI.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: Classifier labels self_harm → fixed policy response path, no tools.

docs.title: Structured LLM router
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Literal

class Route(BaseModel):
    intent: Literal["billing", "tech", "other"]
    confidence: float

async def classify(message: str) -> Route:
    resp = await client.beta.chat.completions.parse(
        model="gpt-4o-mini",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "Classify support intent."},
            {"role": "user", "content": message},
        ],
        response_format=Route,
    )
    return resp.choices[0].message.parsed

async def dispatch(message: str):
    route = await classify(message)
    if route.confidence < 0.6:
        return await clarify(message)
    return await HANDLERS[route.intent](message)

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Monitor confusion matrix of router labels vs human tags.
  • Version router prompts like any other prompt.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Cache embeddings for classifier.
  • Short-circuit rules before any model call.

docs.title: Cost Considerations
docs.text:
• Routing calls should be cheaper than main calls.
  • Avoid double-LLM when rules suffice.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Never let the router disable authz.
  • Jailbreak attempts → safety path.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Rules before models.
  2. Explicit unknown/fallback intent.
  3. Thresholds from eval, not vibes.
  4. Log route + confidence on every request.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Infinite clarify loops
  • Routing only in the system prompt of a single call
  • No evaluation set for intents
  • Using the same large model for routing and answering always

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text: Q: How do you evaluate a router? A: Labeled intent dataset; track precision/recall per class, plus downstream task success and cost after routing.

docs.text: When control flow branches, loops, and pauses for humans, model it as an explicit graph with state and checkpoints — not a spaghetti script.
