docs.title: Python Basics
docs.text: What Python is, how programs run, and the mental model you need before writing real code.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Python is a high-level, interpreted, dynamically typed programming language that emphasizes readability. You write .py source files; the CPython interpreter (the common default) compiles them to bytecode and runs them on a virtual machine.

Python basics covers: running code, program structure, indentation, comments, input/output, expressions vs statements, and the if __name__ == "__main__" pattern.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: AI tooling (NumPy, PyTorch, FastAPI, OpenAI SDKs, LangGraph) is Python-first. Weak basics create endless IndentationError, import, and "why didn't this run?" issues later.

docs.title: How Python runs code
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  S[.py source] --> C[Compile to bytecode]
  C --> V[Python VM executes]
  V --> O[Output / side effects]

docs.title: Types of Python programs
docs.text: Kind Description Example Script Runs top-to-bottom python train.py Module Imported by others import utils Package Folder of modules mypkg/ REPL / notebook Interactive python, Jupyter

docs.title: Core syntax rules
docs.text:
1. Indentation defines blocks (4 spaces). No braces for blocks.
  2. Case-sensitive — Name and name differ.
  3. Comments start with #.
  4. Names bind to objects; types live on objects.

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
# Smallest useful program
print("Hello, AI Engineering")  # writes to stdout

answer = 2 + 2                  # assignment; right side is an expression
print("2 + 2 =", answer)

# Typical script layout
import sys

APP_NAME = "demo"

def greet(name: str) -> str:
    # Return a greeting string
    return f"Welcome, {name}!"

def main() -> None:
    print(greet("Samad"))
    print("Python:", sys.version.split()[0])

# Runs only when executed as a script (not on import)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Indentation creates blocks
score = 85
if score >= 80:
    grade = "A"
    print("Great job")
else:
    grade = "B"
print("Grade:", grade)

docs.title: Variables & Data Types
docs.text: Names, objects, and Python's built-in data types — how values live in memory and how to choose the right type.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A variable is a name bound to an object. Assignment (name = value) creates or rebinds the name. Python is dynamically typed: the same name can later point to a different type.

A data type describes what an object is (int, str, list, …) and which operations it supports.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Hold config, user input, model outputs, API payloads
  • Pick types that match meaning (bool vs 0/1)
  • Understand mutability to avoid shared-state bugs

docs.title: Binding model
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  N[Name x] --> O[Object 42]
  N2[Rebind x] --> O2[Object hello]
x = 42
y = x           # y refers to same int
x = "hello"     # x rebound; y still 42
print(y)        # 42

docs.title: Built-in types
docs.text: Category Types Mutable? Numeric int, float, complex No Boolean bool No Text str No Sequences list, tuple, range only list Sets set, frozenset only set Mapping dict Yes Null None No Binary bytes, bytearray only bytearray

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
age = 30                      # int (arbitrary precision)
temp = 36.6                   # float
ready = True                  # bool
result = None                 # absence of value

name = "Samad"                # str (Unicode)
nums = [1, 2, 3]              # list — mutable
point = (10, 20)              # tuple — immutable
unique = {1, 2, 2}            # set → {1, 2}
user = {"id": 1, "role": "admin"}  # dict

# Always compare None with 'is'
if result is None:
    print("no result")

print(type(name), isinstance(name, str))
as_int = int("42")            # conversion; may raise ValueError

# Mutability: aliases see in-place changes
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)          # [1, 2, 3]

c = a.copy()      # independent shallow copy
c.append(4)
print(a, c)       # [1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3, 4]

docs.text:

MAX_RETRIES = 3      # constant by convention
_internal = True     # "private" by convention

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• == None instead of is None
  • Assuming floats are exact for money (use decimal)
  • Mutating shared lists unintentionally

docs.title: Operators
docs.text: Symbols and keywords that compute, compare, assign, and combine values — arithmetic through walrus and unpacking.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An operator performs an operation on one or more operands. Python includes arithmetic, comparison, logical, bitwise, assignment, membership, identity, and the walrus operator.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Calculations (scores, budgets, sizes)
  • Conditions for branching and loops
  • Compact updates (+=)
  • Membership tests (in)

docs.title: Categories
docs.text: Category Examples Arithmetic + - * / // % ** Comparison == != < > <= >= Logical and or not Bitwise & \| ^ ~ << >> Assignment = += -= *= Membership in not in Identity is is not Walrus :=

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
a, b = 17, 5
print(a + b, a - b, a * b)   # 22 12 85
print(a / b)                  # 3.4 true division → float
print(a // b, a % b)          # 3 2 floor + remainder
print(a ** 2)                 # 289

print(0.1 + 0.2)              # float imprecision demo

x = 10
print(x == 10, 1 < x <= 10)   # True True (chained compare)

skills = ["python", "rag"]
print("rag" in skills)

a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
print(a == b, a is b)         # True False (value vs identity)

count = 0
count += 1
first, *rest = [10, 20, 30]
print(first, rest)            # 10 [20, 30]

# Walrus: assign inside a condition (3.8+)
text = "token_count=128"
if (n := text.split("=")[-1]).isdigit():
    print("tokens:", int(n))

docs.title: Precedence tip
docs.text: When unsure, use parentheses. 2 + 3 * 4 is 14; (2 + 3) * 4 is 20.

docs.title: Conditional Statements
docs.text: Branching with if / elif / else, truthiness, ternary expressions, and structural pattern matching.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Conditional statements choose code paths based on whether conditions hold. Python provides if / elif / else, ternary expressions, and (3.10+) match / case.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Validate inputs and fail fast
  • Route requests by status, role, or intent
  • Feature flags and environment checks

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Form Use if Single branch if/else Binary choice if/elif/else Multi-way Ternary Tiny expression choice match Structured dispatch 
flowchart TD
  C{condition?} -->|True| A[if block]
  C -->|False| E{elif?}
  E -->|True| B[elif block]
  E -->|False| D[else block]

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
def letter_grade(score: int) -> str:
    if score < 0 or score > 100:
        raise ValueError("score must be 0..100")
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    elif score >= 80:
        return "B"
    elif score >= 70:
        return "C"
    else:
        return "D/F"

print(letter_grade(92))

# Truthiness: empty containers, 0, None, "" are falsy
items = []
if not items:
    print("empty")

latency_ms = 120
tier = "fast" if latency_ms < 200 else "slow"  # ternary
print(tier)

# Guard clauses beat deep nesting
user = {"active": True, "role": "admin"}
if not user:
    raise ValueError("missing user")
if not user.get("active"):
    raise PermissionError("inactive")
if user.get("role") != "admin":
    raise PermissionError("admins only")
print("admin panel")

def handle_event(event: dict) -> str:
    match event:  # Python 3.10+
        case {"type": "login", "user": str(name)}:
            return f"welcome {name}"
        case {"type": "error", "code": int(code)} if code >= 500:
            return "server fault"
        case _:
            return "unknown"

print(handle_event({"type": "login", "user": "samad"}))

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Monster elif chains → use dict dispatch
  • Treating 0 as "missing" when zero is valid data

def pick_model(task: str, premium: bool) -> str:
    task = task.lower().strip()
    if task in {"embed", "embedding"}:
        return "text-embedding-3-large"
    if task == "chat" and premium:
        return "gpt-4.1"
    if task == "chat":
        return "gpt-4.1-mini"
    if task == "classify":
        return "small-classifier"
    return "gpt-4.1-mini"  # safe default

print(pick_model("chat", premium=True))

docs.title: Dict dispatch alternative
docs.text:
ROUTES = {
    "embed": lambda premium: "text-embedding-3-large",
    "chat": lambda premium: "gpt-4.1" if premium else "gpt-4.1-mini",
}

def pick_model2(task: str, premium: bool) -> str:
    fn = ROUTES.get(task)
    if fn is None:
        return "gpt-4.1-mini"
    return fn(premium)

docs.title: Loops
docs.text: Repeat work with for and while — iteration patterns, else clauses, nested loops, and when to stop looping.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A loop repeatedly executes a block of code. Python’s main loops are:

  • for — iterate over an iterable (list, string, range, file, …)
  • while — repeat while a condition stays true

Related control keywords: break (exit), continue (skip to next iteration), and optional else on loops (runs if no break).

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Process batches of documents, tokens, or API pages
  • Retry with backoff
  • Aggregate metrics, build indexes, stream lines from files

docs.title: Types / patterns
docs.text:
Pattern Tool Notes Counted loop for i in range(n) Prefer over C-style indexes Item loop for item in seq Idiomatic Index + item enumerate When you need positions Parallel iterables zip Same-length pairing Conditional repeat while Unknown iteration count Infinite + break while True Servers, CLIs, polls 
flowchart TD
  S[Start] --> T{items left / condition?}
  T -->|yes| B[Loop body]
  B --> T
  T -->|no| E[After loop]

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
# for over a sequence
models = ["gpt", "claude", "llama"]
for m in models:
    print("provider family:", m)

# range: 0..4
for i in range(5):
    print(i, end=" ")
print()

# enumerate — index + value
for i, m in enumerate(models, start=1):
    print(f"{i}. {m}")

# zip — iterate in parallel
names = ["a", "b"]
scores = [0.9, 0.7]
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(name, score)

# while + break/continue
attempts = 0
while attempts < 5:
    attempts += 1
    if attempts == 2:
        continue          # skip the rest of this iteration
    if attempts == 4:
        print("stopping early")
        break             # leave the loop
    print("attempt", attempts)
else:
    # runs only if loop did NOT break
    print("finished without break")

# Nested loops — prefer clarity; extract helpers if deep
matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
total = 0
for row in matrix:
    for cell in row:
        total += cell
print(total)  # 10

# Comprehension alternative when building a collection (see topic 13)
flat = [cell for row in matrix for cell in row]

# Practical: paginated API-style loop
def fetch_pages():
    page = 1
    while True:
        # pretend API returns [] when done
        batch = [f"doc-{page}"] if page <= 3 else []
        if not batch:
            break
        for doc in batch:
            yield doc
        page += 1

print(list(fetch_pages()))

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Fix Mutating a list while iterating it Iterate over a copy or build a new list while True without break Always define an exit Using range(len(xs)) always Iterate items directly unless you need indexes Infinite loop on wrong condition Print/log the condition while debugging

docs.title: Performance notes
docs.text:
• for x in huge_list is fine; converting everything to a list first may not be
  • Prefer generators/iterators for large streams (topics 14–15)

docs.title: Worked example: batching
docs.text:
def batched(xs: list[str], size: int):
    """Yield lists of length <= size."""
    batch: list[str] = []
    for x in xs:
        batch.append(x)
        if len(batch) == size:
            yield batch
            batch = []
    if batch:
        yield batch

docs = [f"d{i}" for i in range(10)]
for b in batched(docs, 3):
    print("embed batch", b)

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Define reusable blocks of logic with parameters, returns, defaults, *args/**kwargs, and clean function design.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A function is a named, reusable block of code that can accept parameters, perform work, and optionally return a value. Functions are first-class objects in Python: you can pass them, store them, and return them.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Avoid copy-paste
  • Isolate testable units
  • Express clear inputs/outputs at module boundaries
  • Build APIs of your application layer

docs.title: Types of parameters
docs.text:
Kind Syntax Meaning Positional def f(a, b) Order matters Keyword f(a=1, b=2) Call by name Default def f(a, b=0) Optional at call site Var-positional *args Extra positional → tuple Var-keyword **kwargs Extra keywords → dict Keyword-only def f(a, *, b) b must be keyword Positional-only def f(a, /, b) a must be positional (3.8+) 
flowchart LR
  Call[Caller] --> Args[Bind arguments]
  Args --> Body[Execute body]
  Body --> Ret[Return value or None]

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Return the sum of a and b."""
    return a + b

print(add(2, 3))
print(add(b=5, a=1))   # keyword call

# Defaults — evaluated ONCE at definition time (mutable default pitfall!)
def append_item(item, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None:       # correct pattern
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(append_item("a"))
print(append_item("b"))      # fresh list each time when using None

# *args and **kwargs
def debug_log(message: str, *args, **kwargs):
    print("MSG:", message)
    print("ARGS:", args)
    print("KW:", kwargs)

debug_log("run", 1, 2, level="info", ok=True)

# Keyword-only and return multiple values (tuple packing)
def split_name(full: str, *, lower: bool = False) -> tuple[str, str]:
    first, last = full.split(" ", 1)
    if lower:
        return first.lower(), last.lower()
    return first, last

f, l = split_name("Ada Lovelace", lower=True)
print(f, l)

# Early return clarifies control flow
def normalize_score(score: float | None) -> float:
    if score is None:
        return 0.0
    if score < 0:
        return 0.0
    if score > 1:
        return 1.0
    return score

docs.title: Design guidelines
docs.text:
1. One job per function (or a clear facade)
  2. Pure when possible — same inputs → same outputs, no hidden I/O
  3. Explicit returns — don’t rely on accidental None
  4. Type hints on public functions (topic 27)
  5. Docstrings for non-obvious behavior

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Mutable default arguments (def f(xs=[]))
  • Too many parameters → use a dataclass/TypedDict
  • Side effects hidden behind innocent names like get_* that also write DB

docs.title: Worked example: prompt builder
docs.text:
def build_prompt(
    question: str,
    contexts: list[str],
    *,
    max_contexts: int = 4,
    system: str = "Answer using only the context.",
) -> str:
    chosen = contexts[:max_contexts]
    context_block = "\n\n".join(
        f"[{i}] {c}" for i, c in enumerate(chosen, 1)
    )
    return (
        f"{system}\n\n"
        f"Context:\n{context_block}\n\n"
        f"Question: {question.strip()}\n"
        f"Answer:"
    )

print(build_prompt("What is RAG?", ["Retrieval...", "Generation..."]))

docs.title: Scope & Namespaces
docs.text: LEGB rule, global/nonlocal, name binding, and how Python finds names at runtime.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A namespace is a mapping from names to objects (implemented as dicts under the hood for many scopes). Scope is the textual region where a name is visible.

Python resolves names with the LEGB rule:

  1. Local — function body
  2. Enclosing — outer function(s)
  3. Global — module level
  4. Built-in — len, range, Exception, …

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Avoid accidental globals
  • Write correct closures and decorators
  • Debug UnboundLocalError and shadowing bugs

docs.title: Types of scopes
docs.text:
Scope Created by Lifetime Built-in Interpreter Process Global Module Module lifetime Enclosing Nested def While outer function exists Local Function / comprehension Call / evaluation 
flowchart TB
  B[Built-in] --> G[Global module]
  G --> E[Enclosing function]
  E --> L[Local function]

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
APP = "playbook"          # global

def show():
    print(APP)            # read global OK

def rebind_wrong():
    # Uncommenting next line without global makes APP local → UnboundLocalError on print
    # APP = "x"
    print(APP)

show()

counter = 0

def bump():
    global counter        # needed to ASSIGN to global
    counter += 1

bump(); bump()
print(counter)            # 2

def outer():
    total = 0

    def inner(n):
        nonlocal total    # assign to enclosing scope
        total += n
        return total

    return inner

acc = outer()
print(acc(5), acc(3))     # 5 8

# Shadowing built-ins — avoid
def bad(list):            # shadows built-in list
    return list

# Prefer
def good(items):
    return list(items)

# Comprehension scope (Python 3): loop variable does not leak
squares = [i * i for i in range(3)]
# print(i)  # NameError in Python 3

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Symptom Cause UnboundLocalError Assigned locally later, so read is treated as local Unexpected global mutation Forgot that mutable globals are shared Closure late-binding lambda: i in a loop captures final i — use default arg lambda i=i: i

docs.title: Strings
docs.text: Text in Python — creation, indexing, methods, formatting, encoding, and practical string processing.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A string (str) is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters. Once created, you cannot change a character in place; “modifications” create new strings.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Prompts, messages, logs, file paths (prefer pathlib for paths)
  • Parsing and formatting API payloads
  • Normalization before embedding/tokenization

docs.title: Types / related text types
docs.text: Type Meaning str Unicode text bytes Raw bytes bytearray Mutable bytes

docs.title: Creation & essentials
docs.text:
s1 = "hello"
s2 = 'hello'                 # same
s3 = """multi
line"""                      # triple quotes
raw = r"C:\new\to"           # raw: backslashes kept
print(len(s1), s1[0], s1[-1])
print(s1[1:4])               # slicing "ell"
# s1[0] = "H"                # TypeError — immutable

docs.title: Methods you will use constantly
docs.text:
text = "  Retrieval-Augmented Generation  "
print(text.strip())
print(text.lower())
print(text.replace("Generation", "Gen"))
print("Augmented" in text)
parts = "a,b,c".split(",")
print(parts, ",".join(parts))
print("score:42".partition(":"))
print("file.md".endswith(".md"))
print("42".isdigit())

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
name, score = "rag", 0.87
# f-strings (preferred)
print(f"{name} score={score:.2%}")

# format / %
print("{}={}".format(name, score))
print("%s=%.2f" % (name, score))

docs.title: Encoding
docs.text:
s = "café"
b = s.encode("utf-8")        # str → bytes
print(b)
print(b.decode("utf-8"))     # bytes → str

# Always know your encoding at I/O boundaries (files, HTTP)

docs.title: Practical patterns
docs.text:
def normalize_query(q: str) -> str:
    q = q.strip().lower()
    q = " ".join(q.split())  # collapse whitespace
    return q

def truncate(s: str, n: int, suffix: str = "...") -> str:
    if len(s) <= n:
        return s
    return s[: n - len(suffix)] + suffix

print(normalize_query("  Hello   World "))
print(truncate("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz", 10))

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building huge strings with + in a loop → use "".join(parts) or io.StringIO
  • Mixing str and bytes
  • Using string paths instead of pathlib.Path for filesystem work

docs.title: Worked example: light PII mask
docs.text:
def mask_email(text: str) -> str:
    parts = text.split()
    out = []
    for p in parts:
        if "@" in p and "." in p:
            name, _, domain = p.partition("@")
            out.append(name[:1] + "***@" + domain)
        else:
            out.append(p)
    return " ".join(out)

print(mask_email("contact me at ada@example.com thanks"))

  2. Truncate a prompt preview to 80 chars with ....
  3. Encode/decode a UTF-8 string containing non-ASCII characters.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text: Ordered, mutable sequences — creating, indexing, slicing, methods, copying, and list algorithms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A list is an ordered, mutable sequence that can hold heterogeneous objects. Lists are the workhorse collection for dynamic ordered data.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Batches of records, messages, chunks
  • Stacks/queues (with care)
  • Accumulating results during processing

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text: Property List Ordered Yes Mutable Yes Indexed Yes (O(1) access) Allow duplicates Yes Allow mixed types Yes (prefer homogeneity in practice)

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
xs = [10, 20, 30]
xs.append(40)             # add at end
xs.insert(1, 15)          # insert at index
xs.extend([50, 60])       # add many
print(xs.pop())           # remove & return last
xs.remove(15)             # remove first matching value
print(xs)
print(xs[0], xs[-1], xs[1:3])

# Sorting
scores = [0.2, 0.9, 0.5]
print(sorted(scores))           # new list
scores.sort(reverse=True)       # in-place
print(scores)

rows = [{"id": 2, "s": 0.1}, {"id": 1, "s": 0.8}]
rows.sort(key=lambda r: r["s"], reverse=True)
print(rows)

# Copying
a = [[1], [2]]
b = a                 # alias
c = a.copy()          # shallow copy
import copy
d = copy.deepcopy(a)  # deep copy
a[0].append(99)
print(b, c, d)        # b&c see inner change; d does not

# As stack / queue
stack = []
stack.append("a"); stack.append("b")
print(stack.pop())                # LIFO → b

from collections import deque
q = deque(["a", "b"])
q.append("c")
print(q.popleft())                # FIFO → a

# Idiomatic building
chunks = []
for i in range(3):
    chunks.append(f"chunk-{i}")
# Prefer comprehension when mapping/filtering simply (topic 13)

docs.title: Complexity (amortized)
docs.text: Op Cost Index / append O(1) Insert/pop front O(n) Membership x in list O(n) — use set if frequent

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• list = ... shadowing built-in
  • Shallow copy when nested mutables need isolation
  • Using lists for heavy membership tests

docs.title: Worked example: top-k hits
docs.text:
hits = [
    {"id": "a", "score": 0.4},
    {"id": "b", "score": 0.9},
    {"id": "c", "score": 0.7},
]

def top_k(rows: list[dict], k: int) -> list[dict]:
    ranked = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r["score"], reverse=True)
    return ranked[:k]

print(top_k(hits, 2))

docs.title: Tuples
docs.text: Immutable ordered sequences — records, multiple returns, dictionary keys, and tuple unpacking.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A tuple is an ordered, immutable sequence. After creation, you cannot add/remove/change elements (but mutable objects inside a tuple can still mutate).

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Fixed records (x, y)
  • Multiple return values
  • Dict keys / set elements (if contents are hashable)
  • Safer public APIs (“don’t mutate this”)

docs.title: Tuple vs list
docs.text: Tuple List Mutable No Yes Syntax (1, 2) [1, 2] Hashable If elements are No Intent Fixed structure Grow/shrink

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
point = (3, 4)
# parentheses optional in many assignments:
point2 = 3, 4
singleton = (42,)         # trailing comma required for 1-tuple
empty = ()

print(point[0], len(point))
x, y = point              # unpacking
print(x, y)

def min_max(xs: list[int]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    return min(xs), max(xs)

lo, hi = min_max([3, 1, 7])
print(lo, hi)

# Tuple as dict key
locations = {
    (0, 0): "origin",
    (1, 2): "A",
}
print(locations[(1, 2)])

# Immutable container, mutable content
t = ([1, 2], [3, 4])
t[0].append(99)           # allowed — list inside changes
print(t)
# t[0] = [0]              # TypeError — cannot rebind slot

# namedtuple / typing.NamedTuple for clarity
from typing import NamedTuple

class Chunk(NamedTuple):
    doc_id: str
    text: str
    score: float

c = Chunk("d1", "hello", 0.9)
print(c.text, c.score)

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting comma in singleton (42) is just 42
  • Expecting tuples to deep-freeze contents

docs.title: Sets
docs.text: Unordered collections of unique hashable items — membership, algebra, and deduplication.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A set is an unordered collection of unique hashable elements. Membership tests and deduplication are typically much faster than with lists (O(1) average).

frozenset is an immutable set (hashable; can be a dict key).

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Deduplicate IDs/tokens
  • Fast membership (if user_id in allowed)
  • Set algebra: intersection/union for tags, permissions, vocabularies

docs.title: Types
docs.text: Type Mutable Hashable set Yes No frozenset No Yes

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
skills = {"python", "rag", "python"}
print(skills)                      # {"python", "rag"}

skills.add("agents")
skills.discard("missing")          # no error if absent
print("rag" in skills)             # True fast membership

a = {1, 2, 3}
b = {3, 4}
print(a | b)                       # union
print(a & b)                       # intersection
print(a - b)                       # difference
print(a ^ b)                       # symmetric difference
print(a <= {1, 2, 3, 4})           # subset

# Deduplicate while preserving order (dict trick 3.7+)
items = ["a", "b", "a", "c"]
unique_ordered = list(dict.fromkeys(items))
print(unique_ordered)

# frozenset as dict key
groups = {
    frozenset(["admin", "user"]): "mixed",
    frozenset(["admin"]): "admins",
}
print(groups[frozenset(["user", "admin"])])

# Only hashables allowed
# {{1, 2}}           # TypeError
ok = { (1, 2), (3, 4) }            # tuples of immutables OK

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Relying on set iteration order for logic (order is insertion-based but treat as unordered conceptually)
  • Putting lists inside sets
  • Using sets when you need counts → collections.Counter

docs.title: Dictionaries
docs.text: Key–value maps — the central data structure for records, configs, JSON-like data, and fast lookups.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A dictionary (dict) maps hashable keys to values. In modern CPython (3.7+), dicts preserve insertion order.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• JSON-like objects and API payloads
  • Indexes: id → record
  • Configuration and feature flags
  • Counting and grouping (Counter, defaultdict)

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text: Property Dict Keys unique Yes Keys hashable Required Values any object Yes Lookup by key Average O(1) Ordered (3.7+) Insertion order

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
user = {"id": 1, "name": "Samad", "roles": ["admin"]}
print(user["name"])
print(user.get("email"))              # None if missing
print(user.get("email", "n/a"))

user["email"] = "a@b.com"             # insert/update
user.setdefault("plan", "free")      # set if absent
print(user.keys(), user.values())

for k, v in user.items():
    print(k, "=>", v)

# Merging (3.9+| )
defaults = {"temperature": 0.2, "max_tokens": 512}
overrides = {"temperature": 0.0}
cfg = defaults | overrides
print(cfg)

# unpacking merge
cfg2 = {**defaults, **overrides}

from collections import defaultdict, Counter

# Grouping
rows = [("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("a", 3)]
groups = defaultdict(list)
for k, v in rows:
    groups[k].append(v)
print(dict(groups))

# Counting
print(Counter(["rag", "rag", "agent"]))

# Dict comprehension
scores = {"a": 0.9, "b": 0.2, "c": 0.7}
passed = {k: v for k, v in scores.items() if v >= 0.5}
print(passed)

# JSON round-trip pattern
import json
payload = {"query": "what is rag?", "k": 5}
raw = json.dumps(payload)
back = json.loads(raw)
print(back["k"])

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• KeyError — use .get or in checks
  • Using unhashable keys (list)
  • Mutating dict while iterating keys (iterate over list(d))

docs.title: Worked example: inverted index sketch
docs.text:
docs = {
    "d1": "rag retrieval generation",
    "d2": "agents tools planning",
}

inverted: dict[str, set[str]] = {}
for doc_id, text in docs.items():
    for token in text.split():
        inverted.setdefault(token, set()).add(doc_id)

print(sorted(inverted["rag"]))   # ['d1']
print(inverted.get("tools"))     # {'d2'}

docs.text:
1. Merge two config dicts with overrides winning.
  2. Count word frequencies with Counter.
  3. Invert a dict safely (detect collisions).

docs.title: List/Set/Dictionary Comprehensions
docs.text: Compact, readable ways to build collections from iterables with optional filters — and when not to use them.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A comprehension is syntactic sugar for building a list, set, or dict from an iterable, optionally filtering elements. There are also generator expressions (lazy) with ().

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Map/filter transforms in one readable line
  • Build vocabularies, indexes, filtered batches
  • Keep functional-style transforms local and clear

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Form Example List [x*2 for x in xs if x > 0] Set {x.lower() for x in names} Dict {k: v for k, v in pairs} Generator expr (x*2 for x in xs) 
flowchart LR
  I[Iterable] --> F[Optional filter]
  F --> M[Map expression]
  M --> C[Collection / generator]

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
squares = [n * n for n in nums]
evens = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
print(squares, evens)

# Equivalent loop for mental model
squares2 = []
for n in nums:
    squares2.append(n * n)

names = ["Ada", "alan", "Ada"]
unique_lower = {n.lower() for n in names}
print(unique_lower)

pairs = [("a", 1), ("b", 2)]
d = {k: v for k, v in pairs}
print(d)

# Dict invert (last wins on collisions)
inv = {v: k for k, v in d.items()}

# Nested — flatten matrix
matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
flat = [c for row in matrix for c in row]
print(flat)

# Keep nested comprehensions shallow; extract helper if complex

# Generator expression — lazy, memory friendly
total = sum(n * n for n in range(1000))
print(total)

# Walrus in comprehension (3.8+)
raw = ["1", "x", "3"]
vals = [y for x in raw if (y := x.isdigit() and int(x))]
# cleaner approach:
vals = [int(x) for x in raw if x.isdigit()]
print(vals)

docs.title: When NOT to use comprehensions
docs.text:
• Multi-step logic with side effects (logging, I/O) → use a normal loop
  • Deep nesting that hurts readability
  • Building something that isn’t a collection

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using a list comprehension only for side effects: [print(x) for x in xs] → just loop
  • Accidental nested complexity

docs.title: Iterators & Iterables
docs.text: The iteration protocol — iterables, iterators, next(), and how for-loops really work.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
• An iterable can return an iterator (__iter__), e.g. list, str, dict, file, range.
  • An iterator produces the next value (__next__) and is exhausted when StopIteration is raised.

for x in xs roughly does: it = iter(xs) then repeatedly next(it).

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Stream large datasets without loading everything
  • Custom iteration APIs
  • Understand generators, map, and zip

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Iterable -->|iter| Iterator
  Iterator -->|next| Value
  Iterator -->|exhausted| StopIteration

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
xs = [10, 20, 30]
it = iter(xs)                 # list iterator
print(next(it), next(it))
print(next(it))
# next(it) → StopIteration

# for handles StopIteration for you
for v in xs:
    print(v)

# Many built-ins return iterators/views
d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
print(iter(d.keys()))

# zip/map are iterators (consume once)
z = zip([1, 2], ["a", "b"])
print(list(z))
print(list(z))                # empty — already consumed

# Custom iterable
class CountDown:
    def __init__(self, start: int):
        self.start = start

    def __iter__(self):
        n = self.start
        while n > 0:
            yield n           # generator makes an iterator
            n -= 1

print(list(CountDown(3)))

# itertools helpers
import itertools
print(list(itertools.islice(range(1000), 0, 5)))
print(list(itertools.chain([1, 2], [3, 4])))

docs.title: Iterable vs iterator
docs.text: Iterable Iterator iter() returns iterator often returns self next() usually no yes Reusable often yes (list) usually one-shot

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Exhausting an iterator then reusing it
  • Calling next without default: next(it, None) avoids exceptions when desired

docs.text: Lazy sequences with yield — generator functions, generator expressions, and streaming pipelines.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A generator is a function that uses yield to produce a sequence of values lazily. Calling it returns a generator iterator without running the body until you iterate.

Generator expressions (expr for x in xs) create anonymous generators.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Stream large files / token batches / API pages
  • Pipeline transforms with low memory
  • Infinite sequences with care (itertools.count)

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Kind How Generator function def f(): yield ... Generator expression (x for x in xs) yield from Delegate to sub-iterator 
flowchart LR
  Call[Call generator fn] --> G[Generator object]
  G -->|next| Y[Run to next yield]
  Y --> G
  G -->|done| S[StopIteration]

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
def countdown(n: int):
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1

g = countdown(3)
print(next(g), next(g), next(g))
print(list(countdown(3)))

def read_lines(path: str):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            yield line.rstrip("\n")

# Composition: pipeline
def non_empty(lines):
    for line in lines:
        if line.strip():
            yield line

def numbered(lines):
    for i, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
        yield f"{i}: {line}"

# Example with in-memory data instead of file
sample = ["a", "", "b"]
pipe = numbered(non_empty(iter(sample)))
print(list(pipe))

# yield from
def concat(a, b):
    yield from a
    yield from b

print(list(concat([1, 2], [3])))

# Generator expression
squares = (n * n for n in range(5))
print(sum(squares))
# sum(squares) again → 0 because exhausted

# send / generator as coroutine (advanced peek)
def accumulator():
    total = 0
    while True:
        x = yield total
        if x is None:
            break
        total += x

acc = accumulator()
next(acc)                 # prime
print(acc.send(5))
print(acc.send(3))

docs.title: vs lists
docs.text: Generator List Memory Lazy Eager Reusable No (one-shot) Yes Indexing No Yes Len No (generally) Yes

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting generators to restart automatically
  • Using generators when you need random access / len

docs.title: Lambda Functions
docs.text: Small anonymous functions with lambda — where they shine and where a def is clearer.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A lambda is a small anonymous function expressed as a single expression:

lambda parameters: expression

It returns the expression’s value. Lambdas cannot contain statements (if blocks, assignments as statements, etc.).

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Short key= functions for sort / min / max
  • Tiny callbacks in map / filter (or prefer comprehensions)
  • Inline adapters when defining a full def is noisier

docs.title: Types / forms
docs.text: Form Example One arg lambda x: x*2 Multi arg lambda a, b: a+b No arg lambda: 42 With default lambda x, n=1: x+n

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
double = lambda x: x * 2
print(double(5))

# Sorting
rows = [{"name": "b", "score": 0.2}, {"name": "a", "score": 0.9}]
rows.sort(key=lambda r: r["score"], reverse=True)
print(rows)

# Often clearer with operator.itemgetter
from operator import itemgetter
rows.sort(key=itemgetter("name"))

# In map/filter — comprehension often clearer
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(list(map(lambda n: n * n, nums)))
print([n * n for n in nums])              # preferred by many style guides

# Closure late-binding trap
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])               # [2, 2, 2]

funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)] # bind default at creation
print([f() for f in funcs])               # [0, 1, 2]

# When to use def instead
def normalize(score: float) -> float:
    """Clamp score into [0, 1]."""
    if score < 0:
        return 0.0
    if score > 1:
        return 1.0
    return score

# Multi-branch logic does not belong in lambda

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Single expression only
  • No type-hint-friendly signature as nice as def (can annotate awkwardly)
  • Harder to debug (anonymous in stack traces)

docs.title: Style rule
docs.text: If you need a name, docstring, types, or more than one expression → use def.

docs.title: map(), filter(), reduce()
docs.text: Functional helpers that transform and fold iterables — with idiomatic modern alternatives.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
• map(fn, iterable) — apply fn to each element (lazy iterator)
  • filter(pred, iterable) — keep elements where pred is true (lazy)
  • reduce(fn, iterable[, initializer]) — repeatedly combine elements into one value (functools.reduce)

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Functional pipelines over streams
  • Folding counts/sums/products with custom logic
  • Interop with codebases that prefer FP style

docs.title: Prefer comprehensions?
docs.text: In modern Python, list/dict comprehensions and generator expressions are often clearer than map/filter. Know all three.

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]

# map
print(list(map(str, nums)))
print(list(map(lambda n: n * n, nums)))
print([n * n for n in nums])              # equivalent, often clearer

# filter
print(list(filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, nums)))
print([n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0])

from functools import reduce
import operator

print(reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, nums, 0))   # sum
print(reduce(operator.mul, nums, 1))         # product

# Usually prefer built-ins:
print(sum(nums), min(nums), max(nums))

# Practical: normalize + filter scores
raw = ["0.9", "oops", "0.2", "1.1"]

def to_score(x: str) -> float | None:
    try:
        v = float(x)
    except ValueError:
        return None
    if 0 <= v <= 1:
        return v
    return None

scores = list(filter(lambda v: v is not None, map(to_score, raw)))
# clearer:
scores = [v for v in (to_score(x) for x in raw) if v is not None]
print(scores)

# starmap for unpacking pairs
from itertools import starmap
pairs = [(2, 3), (4, 5)]
print(list(starmap(lambda a, b: a + b, pairs)))

docs.title: Comparison table
docs.text: Goal Functional Idiomatic alternative Transform map comprehension Keep some filter comprehension + if Fold reduce sum/any/all/loop Side effects avoid map plain for

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting list(...) when you need a concrete list (iterators are lazy)
  • Using reduce for simple sums

docs.title: Exception Handling
docs.text: Errors as objects — try/except/else/finally, raising, custom exceptions, and robust failure handling.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An exception signals that something abnormal occurred. Python uses an exception hierarchy rooted at BaseException (you almost always catch Exception, not BaseException).

Exception handling means catching, enriching, converting, or propagating those errors deliberately.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Validate inputs and fail with clear messages
  • Retry transient network errors
  • Ensure files/locks close via finally / context managers
  • Translate low-level errors into domain errors

docs.title: Key forms
docs.text:
Construct Role try Protected block except Handle specific errors else Runs if no exception finally Always runs raise Throw / rethrow raise X from e Chain causes 
flowchart TD
  T[try] -->|error| X[except match?]
  X -->|yes| H[handler]
  X -->|no| P[propagate]
  T -->|ok| E[else]
  H --> F[finally]
  E --> F
  P --> F

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
def parse_int(text: str) -> int:
    try:
        return int(text)
    except ValueError as e:
        raise ValueError(f"not an int: {text!r}") from e

print(parse_int("42"))

# Multiple except + else + finally
values = ["10", "x", "20"]
total = 0
for v in values:
    try:
        n = int(v)
    except ValueError:
        print("skip", v)
    else:
        total += n            # only on success
    finally:
        pass                  # cleanup would go here
print(total)

# Catch specific exceptions — never bare except:
try:
    d = {"a": 1}
    print(d["b"])
except KeyError as e:
    print("missing key", e)

# Custom exception hierarchy
class AppError(Exception):
    """Base for application errors."""

class ConfigError(AppError):
    pass

def load_config(path: str) -> dict:
    if not path.endswith(".json"):
        raise ConfigError(f"unsupported config: {path}")
    return {"path": path}

try:
    load_config("settings.yaml")
except AppError as e:
    print("app failed:", e)

# Don't swallow silently in libraries
def risky():
    try:
        1 / 0
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        # bad: pass
        # better: log + re-raise or return Result
        raise

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Fix Bare except: Catch Exception or specific types Swallowing errors Log and decide: retry, convert, or raise Using exceptions for normal control flow Prefer returning values when expected Catching BaseException Avoid (includes KeyboardInterrupt)

docs.title: File Handling
docs.text: Read and write files safely — text/binary modes, pathlib, context managers, and large-file patterns.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: File handling is reading from and writing to files on disk (or file-like objects). Prefer pathlib.Path + with open(...) so files close even when errors occur.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Load prompts, configs, datasets
  • Write logs, exports, evaluation reports
  • Stream large corpora line-by-line

docs.title: Modes (common)
docs.text: Mode Meaning "r" Read text (default) "w" Write text (truncate) "a" Append text "x" Exclusive create "rb"/"wb" Binary "+" Read/write combo

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("example.txt")

# Write text (UTF-8)
path.write_text("hello\nworld\n", encoding="utf-8")

# Read all
text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
print(text)

# Stream lines (memory friendly)
with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.rstrip())

# JSON / structured data
import json
data_path = Path("data.json")
data_path.write_text(json.dumps({"k": 5}, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
obj = json.loads(data_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
print(obj["k"])

# Binary
bpath = Path("blob.bin")
bpath.write_bytes(b"\x00\x01\x02")
print(bpath.read_bytes())

# Safe write pattern (write temp then replace)
def atomic_write(path: Path, content: str) -> None:
    tmp = path.with_suffix(path.suffix + ".tmp")
    tmp.write_text(content, encoding="utf-8")
    tmp.replace(path)

atomic_write(Path("safe.txt"), "ok\n")

# Directory ops
out = Path("outputs")
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
for p in Path(".").glob("*.md"):
    print("md:", p.name)

docs.title: Always specify encoding
docs.text: On some platforms default encoding is not UTF-8. Always pass encoding="utf-8" for text.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting to close files (use with)
  • Loading a 10GB file with .read()
  • Hard-coded backslashes instead of Path

docs.title: Modules & Packages
docs.text: Organize code into importable units — modules, packages, imports, init.py, and project structure.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
• A module is a single .py file (or built-in/C extension) that you import.
  • A package is a directory of modules (typically with __init__.py) forming a hierarchy.

Imports bind names in your namespace to objects defined elsewhere.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Split large programs into maintainable units
  • Reuse utilities across apps
  • Publish libraries / internal SDKs

docs.title: Types of imports
docs.text:
import math                      # module binding
from math import sqrt            # name binding
from math import sqrt as root    # alias
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

flowchart TB
  App[app.py] -->|import| Pkg[mypkg]
  Pkg --> M1[mypkg.utils]
  Pkg --> M2[mypkg.services]

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
# mypkg/__init__.py
# (re)export convenient API
# from .utils import normalize

# mypkg/utils.py
def normalize(text: str) -> str:
    return " ".join(text.strip().lower().split())

# Relative imports inside a package
# from .utils import normalize
# from ..core import engine

# Absolute imports preferred in apps:
# from mypkg.utils import normalize

# __name__ and scripts
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("running as script")

# Import side effects — keep module import light
# (don't train models at import time)

# sys.path reality check
import sys
print(sys.path[0])    # often the script directory

# Prefer proper packaging / editable installs over path hacks

docs.title: Package layout (simple app)
docs.text:
app/
  pyproject.toml
  src/
    myapp/
      __init__.py
      main.py
      services/
        __init__.py
        rag.py
  tests/
    test_rag.py

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Fix Circular imports Invert dependencies / lazy import / extract shared module Heavy work at import Put in main() / functions sys.path.append chaos Use packages + install editable Wildcard from x import * Explicit imports only

docs.title: Virtual Environments
docs.text: Isolate project dependencies with venv, virtualenv, and uv — why isolation matters and how to use it daily.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A virtual environment is an isolated Python runtime directory with its own python / pip and installed packages. It prevents Project A’s dependencies from breaking Project B.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Keep AI projects (torch, fastapi, langchain) from colliding
  • Reproduce installs per project
  • Safe experimentation without polluting system Python

docs.title: Types / tools
docs.text:
Tool Notes venv Standard library (recommended baseline) virtualenv Third-party predecessor uv venv / uv sync Modern fast tooling Conda Common in data science; different model 
flowchart TB
  Sys[System Python] --> V1[venv project A]
  Sys --> V2[venv project B]
  V1 --> PA[packages A]
  V2 --> PB[packages B]

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
# Create with stdlib venv
python3 -m venv .venv

# Activate (Linux/macOS)
source .venv/bin/activate

# Activate (Windows PowerShell)
# .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# Confirm
which python
python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"

# Deactivate
deactivate

# uv workflow (fast)
uv venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install fastapi httpx

# Useful hygiene
echo ".venv/" >> .gitignore
python -m pip install --upgrade pip

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
1. One venv per project
  2. Never sudo pip install into system Python for app work
  3. Commit lockfiles, not the venv folder
  4. Document Python version (.python-version or requires-python)

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Installing packages while venv is inactive
  • Checking .venv into git
  • Mixing conda base env for everything

docs.title: Package Management
docs.text: Install and pin dependencies with pip, requirements files, pyproject.toml, and lockfiles.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Package management is how you declare, install, upgrade, and lock third-party libraries so environments are reproducible.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Add FastAPI, OpenAI SDK, NumPy, pytest, …
  • Reproduce CI and production installs
  • Avoid “works on my machine” drift

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text: Concept Meaning Distribution package Installable project on PyPI Requirement Constraint like httpx>=0.27 Lockfile Exact versions that were resolved Extra Optional dependency group (dev)

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
# pip basics (inside a venv)
python -m pip install httpx
python -m pip install 'fastapi[standard]'
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

# pyproject.toml (modern packaging)
[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
  "fastapi>=0.115",
  "httpx>=0.27",
  "pydantic>=2.0",
]

[dependency-groups]
dev = ["pytest>=8.0", "ruff>=0.6"]

# uv sync example
uv sync
uv add pydantic
uv add --dev pytest

# requirements style (apps)
fastapi==0.115.0
httpx==0.27.2
# pins for reproducibility; regenerate deliberately

docs.title: Version specifiers
docs.text:
package==1.2.3    # exact
package>=1.2,<2   # compatible range
package~=1.2.3    # compatible release

docs.title: Best practices for AI apps
docs.text:
1. Pin transitive deps in deploy lockfiles
  2. Separate runtime vs dev dependencies
  3. Upgrade intentionally; run tests/evals after
  4. Prefer official provider SDKs + small stack over mega-frameworks by default

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No pins in production
  • Installing with multiple tools into one env chaotically
  • Committing secrets in package config

docs.title: Object-Oriented Programming
docs.text: Classes, objects, inheritance, composition, dunder methods, and when OOP helps AI codebases.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) models software as objects — bundles of state (attributes) and behavior (methods) — created from classes (blueprints).

Python’s OOP is pragmatic: everything is an object, multiple inheritance exists, and composition is often better than deep hierarchies.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Model domain entities (User, Document, Agent, Tool)
  • Share behavior via base classes/mixins carefully
  • Encapsulate invariants and validation

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
Concept Meaning Class Blueprint Instance Concrete object Attribute Data on object/class Method Function on class Inheritance Reuse/specialize Composition Has-a relationships Encapsulation Hide internals (_protected) Polymorphism Same interface, different behavior 
flowchart TB
  C[Class Agent] --> I1[Instance support_agent]
  C --> I2[Instance research_agent]

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
class Document:
    def __init__(self, doc_id: str, text: str) -> None:
        self.doc_id = doc_id
        self.text = text

    def preview(self, n: int = 50) -> str:
        return self.text[:n]

doc = Document("d1", "Retrieval augmented generation ...")
print(doc.preview(20))

# Inheritance
class Chunk(Document):
    def __init__(self, doc_id: str, text: str, index: int) -> None:
        super().__init__(doc_id, text)
        self.index = index

c = Chunk("d1", "hello world", 0)
print(c.doc_id, c.index)

# Composition over deep inheritance
class Embedder:
    def embed(self, text: str) -> list[float]:
        return [float(len(text))]  # toy

class Retriever:
    def __init__(self, embedder: Embedder) -> None:
        self.embedder = embedder

    def query(self, text: str) -> list[float]:
        return self.embedder.embed(text)

print(Retriever(Embedder()).query("rag"))

# Dunder methods
class Score:
    def __init__(self, value: float) -> None:
        self.value = value

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"Score({self.value!r})"

    def __lt__(self, other: "Score") -> bool:
        return self.value < other.value

print(sorted([Score(0.2), Score(0.9)]))

# @property for derived/validated attributes
class User:
    def __init__(self, email: str) -> None:
        self._email = email

    @property
    def email(self) -> str:
        return self._email

    @email.setter
    def email(self, value: str) -> None:
        if "@" not in value:
            raise ValueError("invalid email")
        self._email = value

docs.title: When not to OOP everything
docs.text:
• Simple scripts → functions + dataclasses
  • Deep inheritance trees → hard to change
  • Prefer protocols for interfaces

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• God classes that do everything
  • Overusing inheritance for code reuse
  • Mutable class attributes shared across instances

docs.title: Dataclasses
docs.text: Boilerplate-free data containers with @dataclass — fields, defaults, frozen records, and vs Pydantic.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A dataclass (via @dataclass) is a class auto-generated with __init__, __repr__, comparisons, etc., from annotated fields. Ideal for plain data records.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Request/response internal models
  • Config objects
  • Intermediate pipeline structures (Chunk, Hit, Message)

docs.title: Types / options
docs.text: Option Effect frozen=True Immutable instances slots=True Lower memory (3.10+) order=True Ordering methods kw_only=True Keyword-only fields (3.10+)

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict

@dataclass
class Chunk:
    doc_id: str
    text: str
    score: float = 0.0
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

c = Chunk("d1", "hello", 0.9, tags=["rag"])
print(c)
print(asdict(c))

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ModelRef:
    provider: str
    name: str

m = ModelRef("openai", "gpt-4.1")
# m.name = "x"  # FrozenInstanceError

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Message:
    role: str
    content: str

    def tokens_heuristic(self) -> int:
        return max(1, len(self.content) // 4)

print(Message("user", "hello world").tokens_heuristic())

@dataclass
class BaseEvent:
    type: str

@dataclass
class LoginEvent(BaseEvent):
    user: str

print(LoginEvent(type="login", user="samad"))

docs.text: Tool Validation Best for dataclass Minimal Internal trusted data Pydantic Rich runtime API boundaries TypedDict Type checker only Dict-shaped JSON

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Mutable default tags: list = [] → use field(default_factory=list)
  • Expecting validation like Pydantic

docs.title: Decorators
docs.text: Wrap functions and classes to add behavior — timing, retries, caching, auth checks — without rewriting call sites.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A decorator is a callable that takes a function/class and returns a new callable, usually wrapping it. Syntax sugar: @decorator above a def equals f = decorator(f).

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Logging / timing
  • Retries and circuit breakers
  • Caching (functools.lru_cache)
  • Authz checks on FastAPI routes
  • Registering tools/agents

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Kind Example Function decorator @timer Decorator with args @retry(times=3) Class decorator @dataclass Method decorators @classmethod @staticmethod @property 
flowchart LR
  Call[Caller] --> Wrap[Wrapper]
  Wrap --> Orig[Original function]
  Orig --> Wrap
  Wrap --> Call

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
import time
from functools import wraps

def timer(fn):
    @wraps(fn)  # preserve name/docstring
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        try:
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
        finally:
            ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
            print(f"{fn.__name__} took {ms:.2f} ms")
    return wrapper

@timer
def work(n: int) -> int:
    return sum(range(n))

print(work(100000))

# Decorator with arguments → nested factory
def retry(times: int = 3):
    def deco(fn):
        @wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            last = None
            for attempt in range(1, times + 1):
                try:
                    return fn(*args, **kwargs)
                except Exception as e:
                    last = e
                    print(f"attempt {attempt} failed: {e}")
            raise last
        return wrapper
    return deco

@retry(times=2)
def flaky():
    raise RuntimeError("boom")

from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def fib(n: int) -> int:
    if n < 2:
        return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

print(fib(20))

class Hot:
    count = 0

    @classmethod
    def bump(cls):
        cls.count += 1
        return cls.count

    @staticmethod
    def ping():
        return "pong"

print(Hot.bump(), Hot.ping())

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting @wraps (breaks debugging / FastAPI signatures)
  • Decorators that swallow exceptions silently
  • Heavy side effects at decoration import time

docs.title: Context Managers
docs.text: The with statement — deterministic setup/teardown for files, locks, sessions, and temporary state.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A context manager is an object that defines runtime contexts entered/exited via the with statement. It guarantees cleanup (__exit__) runs even if an exception occurs.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Files, DB connections, HTTP sessions
  • Locks and temporary env vars
  • Timing blocks, tracing spans

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Style How Class-based __enter__ / __exit__ Generator-based @contextmanager Async __aenter__ / __aexit__ / @asynccontextmanager 
flowchart LR
  E[__enter__] --> B[with body]
  B --> X[__exit__]
  B -->|error| X

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
path = Path("cm.txt")
with path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("hello\n")
# file closed here even if write failed

from contextlib import contextmanager
import time

@contextmanager
def timed(label: str):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        print(label, "ms:", (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000)

with timed("sum"):
    sum(range(100000))

class Acquire:
    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name

    def __enter__(self):
        print("acquire", self.name)
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        print("release", self.name)
        return False  # do not suppress exceptions

with Acquire("lock"):
    print("critical section")

# Multiple context managers
from pathlib import Path
p1, p2 = Path("a.txt"), Path("b.txt")
p1.write_text("1", encoding="utf-8")
p2.write_text("2", encoding="utf-8")
with p1.open(encoding="utf-8") as f1, p2.open(encoding="utf-8") as f2:
    print(f1.read(), f2.read())

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Opening files without with
  • Doing heavy work in __enter__ without matching cleanup
  • Suppressing all exceptions in __exit__

docs.title: Type Hints
docs.text: Optional static types for clarity and tooling — annotations, typing constructs, Protocols, and mypy/pyright.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Type hints (annotations) declare expected types for variables, parameters, and returns. They do not enforce types at runtime by default; tools like Pyright / mypy check them statically. Pydantic can validate at runtime on boundaries.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Document APIs for humans and IDEs
  • Catch bugs before production
  • Enable better autocomplete/refactors

docs.title: Common typing constructs
docs.text: Hint Meaning int, str Concrete types list[str] List of strings (3.9+) dict[str, int] Mapping X \| None Optional (3.10+) Iterable[X] Any iterable Callable[[A], R] Function types TypeVar / generics Parametric types Protocol Structural interface TypedDict Dict shape Literal["a","b"] Specific values Any Escape hatch (minimize)

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
def greet(name: str, times: int = 1) -> str:
    return " ".join([f"Hi {name}!"] * times)

print(greet("Samad"))

from collections.abc import Iterable

def mean(xs: Iterable[float]) -> float:
    vals = list(xs)
    return sum(vals) / len(vals)

print(mean([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]))

from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")

def first(xs: list[T]) -> T | None:
    return xs[0] if xs else None

print(first([10, 20]))

from typing import Protocol

class Embedder(Protocol):
    def embed(self, text: str) -> list[float]: ...

class LenEmbedder:
    def embed(self, text: str) -> list[float]:
        return [float(len(text))]

def run(e: Embedder, text: str) -> list[float]:
    return e.embed(text)

print(run(LenEmbedder(), "rag"))

from typing import TypedDict

class Hit(TypedDict):
    doc_id: str
    score: float

hit: Hit = {"doc_id": "d1", "score": 0.9}

docs.title: Gradual typing strategy
docs.text:
1. Annotate public functions first
  2. Keep Any rare
  3. Validate at I/O boundaries (Pydantic)
  4. Run Pyright/mypy in CI

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Thinking hints enforce runtime safety alone
  • Overusing Any
  • Annotating everything privately before APIs stabilize

docs.title: Regular Expressions
docs.text: Pattern matching on text with re — search, match, groups, substitution, and safe usage guidelines.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A regular expression (regex) is a pattern language for matching and extracting text. Python’s standard module is re (and the third-party regex package for advanced Unicode needs).

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Validate simple formats (carefully)
  • Extract fields from logs
  • Light parsing when full grammars are overkill
  • Redacting PII patterns in traces

docs.title: Core operations
docs.text: Function Role re.search First match anywhere re.match Match at start re.fullmatch Entire string re.findall All matches re.finditer Match objects iterator re.sub Substitute re.compile Precompile pattern

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
import re

text = "order id=A-123 status=paid"
m = re.search(r"id=([A-Z]-\d+)", text)
if m:
    print(m.group(1))  # A-123

# Flags
print(re.findall(r"hi", "Hi hi HI", flags=re.IGNORECASE))

# Named groups + verbose flag (single-line pattern for clarity)
pattern = re.compile(
    r"(?P<key>[a-z_]+)=(?P<value>\S+)",
    re.VERBOSE,
)
print(pattern.search("max_tokens=512").groupdict())

# Substitution / redaction
log = "user email=a@b.com ok"
redacted = re.sub(r"[\w.]+@[\w.]+", "<EMAIL>", log)
print(redacted)

# Split
print(re.split(r"\s*,\s*", "a, b,c"))

# Prefer raw strings for patterns
# Good: r"\d+"
# Confusing: "\\d+" vs accidental escape bugs

docs.title: Safety & performance
docs.text:
• Prefer simple string methods when enough (in, startswith, split)
  • Avoid catastrophic backtracking on untrusted input
  • Compile once if used in a hot loop

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Overcomplex regex for nested structures (use a parser)
  • Forgetting raw strings
  • Using regex as the only email validator (too naive or too strict)

docs.title: Functional Programming
docs.text: FP ideas in Python — purity, immutability, higher-order functions, and practical functional style.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Functional programming (FP) emphasizes pure functions (no side effects), immutable data, and functions as values. Python is multi-paradigm: use FP ideas where they improve clarity, not as dogma.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Predictable transforms in data/RAG pipelines
  • Easier testing (pure functions)
  • Safer concurrency (less shared mutable state)

docs.title: Core ideas
docs.text: Idea Meaning Pure function Same inputs → same outputs; no side effects Higher-order fn Takes/returns functions Immutability Prefer new values over mutation Composition Build pipelines from small functions Lazy eval Generators / iterators

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
from collections.abc import Callable

def compose(f: Callable, g: Callable) -> Callable:
    return lambda x: f(g(x))

def normalize(s: str) -> str:
    return " ".join(s.strip().lower().split())

def exclaim(s: str) -> str:
    return s + "!"

pipeline = compose(exclaim, normalize)
print(pipeline("  Hello   RAG "))

# Pure transform vs impure
def add_score_pure(row: dict, delta: float) -> dict:
    return {**row, "score": row["score"] + delta}  # new dict

def add_score_impure(row: dict, delta: float) -> dict:
    row["score"] += delta  # mutates caller data
    return row

from collections.abc import Callable

def rank(items: list[str], key: Callable[[str], float]) -> list[str]:
    return sorted(items, key=key, reverse=True)

print(rank(["aa", "b", "cccc"], key=len))

from functools import partial

def power(base: int, exp: int) -> int:
    return base ** exp

square = partial(power, exp=2)
print(square(5))

from types import MappingProxyType
cfg = MappingProxyType({"temperature": 0.2})
# cfg["temperature"] = 0.0  # TypeError

docs.title: Balance
docs.text:
• FP for transforms; OOP/modules for boundaries; procedures for scripts
  • Prefer readable comprehensions over clever FP chains

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Deep nested reduce nobody can read
  • Pretending Python lists are immutable

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Structured, configurable application logs with the logging module — levels, handlers, formatters, and AI-service practice.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Logging records events about a running program (info, warnings, errors) through the standard logging module (or structured libraries like structlog). Unlike print, logging is configurable by severity, destination, and format.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Debug production issues
  • Audit agent/tool calls (with redaction)
  • Ops alerts on ERROR rates

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
Level Typical use DEBUG Detailed diagnostics INFO Normal milestones WARNING Unexpected but handled ERROR Failure of an operation CRITICAL System unusable 
flowchart LR
  Logger --> Handler1[Console]
  Logger --> Handler2[File]
  Handler1 --> Formatter
  Handler2 --> Formatter

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

logger.info("server starting")
logger.warning("cache miss")
try:
    1 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    logger.exception("division failed")  # includes stack trace

# Per-module loggers (recommended)
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
log.debug("retrieving k=%s", 5)  # lazy % formatting

# Don't log secrets
user_id = "u_123"
logger.info("user=%s key=%s", user_id, "***")  # redact

# Structured-ish key=value (or use structlog/JSON)

docs.title: Unit Testing
docs.text: Verify code with pytest — tests, fixtures, assertions, parametrization, and testing AI boundaries.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Unit testing checks small pieces of code (functions/classes) in isolation to catch regressions early. In Python, pytest is the de facto standard.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Lock parsing/normalization logic
  • Prevent prompt-builder regressions
  • CI gates before deploy
  • Fast feedback while refactoring

docs.title: Types of tests (pyramid)
docs.text: Type Scope Speed Unit One function/module Fast Integration DB/API together Medium E2E / eval Full system / LLM quality Slower

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
# test_normalize.py
def normalize(text: str) -> str:
    return " ".join(text.strip().lower().split())

def test_normalize_collapses_space():
    assert normalize("  Hello   World ") == "hello world"

def test_normalize_empty():
    assert normalize("   ") == ""

import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def sample_docs():
    return [{"id": "1", "text": "rag"}, {"id": "2", "text": "agent"}]

def test_count(sample_docs):
    assert len(sample_docs) == 2

import pytest

@pytest.mark.parametrize("raw,expected", [
    ("42", 42),
    ("0", 0),
])
def test_parse(raw, expected):
    assert int(raw) == expected

import pytest

def test_rejects_negative():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        raise ValueError("nope")

from unittest.mock import Mock

llm = Mock(return_value="ok")
assert llm("hi") == "ok"
llm.assert_called_once_with("hi")

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: Find and fix bugs systematically — prints, logging, pdb/breakpoint, bisecting, and AI-era failure modes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Debugging is the disciplined process of forming hypotheses about incorrect behavior, gathering evidence, and applying a minimal fix. Tools help, but process matters more.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Fix crashes and wrong outputs
  • Diagnose flaky tests
  • Understand production incidents from logs/traces

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text:
Technique When Reproduce minimally Always first print / log values Quick checks breakpoint() / pdb Interactive Bisect / binary search Regressions Git bisect When introduced? Divide & conquer Isolate layer 
flowchart TB

  H --> E[Evidence]
  E --> F[Fix]
  F --> V[Verify + regression test]

docs.text:
def score(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    print("DEBUG xs=", xs)          # temporary

def normalize(scores):
    breakpoint()                    # drops into debugger
    total = sum(scores)
    return [s / total for s in scores]

# pdb commands: n (next), s (step), c (continue), p expr, l, q

def chunk(text: str, size: int) -> list[str]:
    assert size > 0, "size must be positive"
    return [text[i:i+size] for i in range(0, len(text), size)]

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text: Doing overlapping work — concepts of concurrency vs parallelism, and Python’s main tools.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Concurrency means structuring a program so multiple tasks make progress over the same time period (interleaved or parallel). Parallelism means tasks execute at the same instant on multiple CPUs.

In Python:

  • Async I/O — concurrent waiting (network)
  • Threads — concurrent I/O-bound work
  • Processes — parallel CPU-bound work

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Call many LLM/HTTP APIs efficiently
  • Overlap retrieval + rerank prep
  • Parallelize CPU-heavy preprocessing

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  Q[Workload type?] -->|many network waits| A[asyncio / threads]
  Q -->|heavy CPU| P[multiprocessing]
  Q -->|simple script| S[sync is fine]

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Tool Best for GIL impact asyncio Many sockets / HTTP Avoids blocking if truly async threading I/O-bound, blocking libs GIL limits CPU parallelism multiprocessing CPU-bound Separate GILs / processes

docs.title: Code sketch
docs.text:
import time

def sync_sleep():
    time.sleep(0.1)           # blocks thread

# Async sleeps don't block the event loop (see topic 36)
# Threads can run blocking I/O concurrently (topic 34)
# Processes compute in parallel (topic 35)

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Calling blocking I/O inside async event loops
  • Sharing mutable state across threads without locks
  • Assuming threads speed up pure-Python CPU loops

docs.title: Multithreading
docs.text: Threads for overlapping I/O — ThreadPoolExecutor, shared state, locks, and GIL realities.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A thread is a unit of execution within a process sharing memory. Python’s threading and concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor help run blocking I/O concurrently.

Due to the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) in CPython, threads rarely speed up pure-Python CPU work, but they help with I/O waits.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Concurrent HTTP calls with blocking SDKs
  • Background workers in simple apps
  • Parallelizing I/O-bound preprocessing

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
import time

def fetch(n: int) -> str:
    time.sleep(0.2)                 # pretend network I/O
    return f"result-{n}"

t0 = time.perf_counter()
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=5) as pool:
    futures = [pool.submit(fetch, i) for i in range(5)]
    results = [f.result() for f in as_completed(futures)]
print(results)
print("elapsed", time.perf_counter() - t0)

import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def bump():
    global counter
    for _ in range(10000):
        with lock:                  # protect shared mutation
            counter += 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=bump) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(counter)                      # 40000 if locked correctly

import threading
tls = threading.local()

def work():
    tls.req_id = threading.get_ident()
    print("req", tls.req_id)

docs.title: Safety rules
docs.text:
1. Minimize shared mutable state
  2. Use queues (queue.Queue) to pass messages
  3. Don’t kill threads abruptly; use events/flags
  4. Prefer ThreadPoolExecutor over manual threads

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Race conditions without locks
  • Deadlocks (lock ordering)
  • Using threads for CPU-bound Python loops

docs.title: Multiprocessing
docs.text: Process-based parallelism for CPU-bound work — pools, pickling, and process-safe patterns.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Multiprocessing runs code in separate processes, each with its own Python interpreter and GIL. Ideal for CPU-bound parallelism on multiple cores.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• CPU-heavy tokenization/preprocessing
  • Parallel offline evaluation
  • Feature extraction when not already in native libs

docs.title: Tradeoffs
docs.text: Pros Cons True parallel CPU Higher memory Crash isolation Pickling overhead Bypass GIL Harder shared state

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def cpu_heavy(n: int) -> int:
    return sum(i * i for i in range(n))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
        print(list(pool.map(cpu_heavy, [200000] * 4)))

from multiprocessing import Process, Queue

def worker(q: Queue, x: int) -> None:
    q.put(x * x)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    q: Queue = Queue()
    p = Process(target=worker, args=(q, 7))
    p.start()
    p.join()
    print(q.get())

docs.title: Important constraints
docs.text:
1. Guard entrypoints with if __name__ == "__main__": (esp. Windows/mac spawn)
  2. Arguments/results must be picklable
  3. Prefer ProcessPoolExecutor for simple map/submit patterns
  4. Shared memory exists but keep it rare

docs.title: vs threads vs async
docs.text:
• Network fan-out → async/threads
  • Pure Python CPU → processes
  • NumPy/PyTorch often already release GIL / use their own threads

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting __main__ guard → infinite process spawn
  • Huge payloads over queues
  • Assuming processes share memory like threads

docs.title: Asynchronous Programming
docs.text: asyncio event loops, async/await, tasks, and non-blocking I/O for high-concurrency AI services.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Asynchronous programming in Python uses async / await and an event loop (asyncio) to interleave many I/O-bound tasks in one thread without blocking on each wait.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• FastAPI request handlers
  • Concurrent LLM/provider calls
  • Fan-out retrieval + tools
  • Websockets / streaming responses

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
Concept Meaning Coroutine async def function await Pause until awaitable completes Task Scheduled coroutine Event loop Schedules ready tasks async with / for Async CM / iteration 
flowchart LR
  T1[Task A wait IO] --> Loop[Event loop]
  T2[Task B run] --> Loop
  Loop --> T1

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
import asyncio

async def fetch(n: int) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)          # non-blocking sleep
    return f"result-{n}"

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(i) for i in range(5)))
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())

async def bounded_gather(coros, limit: int = 10):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(limit)

    async def run(c):
        async with sem:
            return await c

    return await asyncio.gather(*(run(c) for c in coros))

async def call():
    async with asyncio.timeout(1.0):   # 3.11+
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        return "ok"

import time
import asyncio

async def bad():
    time.sleep(1)                      # blocks everything

async def good():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)

async def read_blocking():
    return await asyncio.to_thread(time.sleep, 0.2)

docs.title: Rules for AI services
docs.text:
1. Use async HTTP clients (httpx.AsyncClient)
  2. Bound concurrency (semaphores) to protect providers
  3. Cancel/timeouts on every external call
  4. Don’t mix blocking SDK calls into async handlers without to_thread

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting await
  • Calling asyncio.run inside running loop
  • CPU-heavy work on the loop thread

docs.title: Memory Management
docs.text: How Python allocates and frees objects — reference counting, GC, and practical memory hygiene.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Python manages memory automatically via reference counting (primary in CPython) plus a cyclic garbage collector for reference cycles. Developers still must avoid retaining huge object graphs unnecessarily.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Stream large datasets instead of loading all
  • Diagnose memory leaks in long-running services
  • Choose structures (slots, generators) wisely

docs.title: Key ideas
docs.text:
Idea Meaning Refcount Object freed when count → 0 Cycle GC Collects unreachable cycles Peak vs leak Spike OK; unbounded growth not __slots__ Restrict attrs; save memory 
flowchart LR
  Alloc[Allocate object] --> Use[References live]
  Use -->|refcount 0| Free[Deallocate]
  Use -->|cycle only| GC[Cycle GC]

docs.title: Code examples
docs.text:
import sys
a = []
b = a
print(sys.getrefcount(a))     # includes temporary refs from the call

def numbers(n):
    for i in range(n):
        yield i

print(sum(numbers(1_000_000)))

class Point:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

p = Point(1, 2)

import gc
gc.collect()

from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def compute(x: int) -> int:
    return x * x

import tracemalloc
tracemalloc.start()
data = [bytearray(1024) for _ in range(1000)]
print(tracemalloc.get_traced_memory())  # current, peak
tracemalloc.stop()

docs.title: Practical hygiene for AI apps
docs.text:
1. Don’t keep all raw documents in memory if you can stream
  2. Bound queues and caches
  3. Watch batch sizes for embeddings
  4. Profile with tracemalloc when needed

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Global lists that grow forever (unbounded caches)
  • Circular references in graphs/caches without weakrefs
  • Copying giant lists accidentally
